Abstract




The first author dedicates the book to his father, mother, wife, son and daughter: Edvard Sargsyan, Gayane Shahinyan, Aleksandra Sawa, Tigran Sargsyan and Nairi Sargsyan.

The second author dedicates the book to his father, mother, wife and son: Phil Trang, Tram Pham, Tran Tran and Shawn Trang.

Chapter 1
Introduction

This manuscript is a contribution to
descriptive inner model theory
, which is the area of set theory that lies between descriptive set theory as developed in
[
24
]
and inner model theory. The main goal of this manuscript is to advance the descriptive inner model theoretic methods to the level of the
\sf{Largest\ Suslin\ Axiom}
(
\sf{LSA}
), which is a strong determinacy axiom asserting that there is a largest Suslin cardinal and that the largest Suslin cardinal is a member of the Solovay sequence. In more concrete terms, our goal is twofold: Firstly develop methods for analyzing the minimal model of
\sf{LSA}
, and secondly, develop methods for building the minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
under various hypotheses such as the
\sf{Proper\ Forcing\ Axiom}
or
\sf{Large\ Cardinals}
. Since the introduction of Steel’s recent manuscript
[
65
]
, the expository paper
[
29
]
and the introduction of
[
37
]
contain all the introductory information we need, here we will not introduce the subject matter of this book and instead will hope that the reader has consulted these sources.

The first problem is an instance of the problem Steel mentions on page xii of
[
65
]
where he writes: “The most important of the remaining open problems is whether, assuming determinacy, there actually are mouse pairs at every appropriate level of logical complexity”. Theorem
10.1.2
shows that the aformentioned problem has a positive solution in the minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
. As explained in any of the sources cited above, the goal for doing this is to show that letting
\Theta
be the least ordinal that is not a surjective image of the reals,
V_{\Theta}^{\rm{HOD}}
as computed inside a determinacy model is a hod premouse. The above sources explain the importance of having a hod premouse representation of
V_{\Theta}^{\rm{HOD}}
.

The second problem amounts to advancing the
\sf{Core\ Model\ Induction}
to the level of
{\sf{LSA}}
. Corollary
12.0.3
constructs the minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
assuming
{\sf{PFA}}
. More dramatically, the paper
[
37
]
, which extends the methods of this manuscript, demonstrates that the
\sf{Core\ Model\ Induction}
, in its current form, cannot be used to go much further than
{\sf{LSA}}
.

Corollary
12.0.3
also builds the minimal model of
\sf{LSA}
directly from large cardinals, namely strongly compact cardinals. However, Theorem
10.3.1
shows that
{\sf{LSA}}
is weaker than a Woodin cardinal that is a limit of Woodin cardinals, and so strong compactness seems to be much more than needed. Nevertheless, while it is widely believed that strongly compact cardinals are consistency wise stronger than a Woodin cardinal that is a limit of Woodin cardinals, this is not yet known.
Still we strongly believe that the methods developed in this manuscript, the methods of
[
1
]
and the main theorem of
[
26
]
can be used to show that assuming the existence of a Woodin cardinal that is a limit of Woodin cardinals, the minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
exists (cf. Definition
1.0.4
).

Historically,
{\sf{LSA}}
was introduced by Woodin in
[
70
, Remark 9.28]
, and it features prominently in Woodin’s
\sf{Ultimate\ L}
framework (see
[
71
, Definition 7.14]
and Axiom I and Axiom II on page 97 of
[
71
]
1
1

1

The requirement in these axioms that there is a strong cardinal which is a limit of Woodin cardinals is only possible if
L(A,{\mathbb{R}})\vDash\sf{LSA}
.
). Theorem
10.3.1
is historically the first proof of the consistency of
{\sf{LSA}}
relative to large cardinals. Cramer and Woodin established the consistency of
{\sf{LSA}}
from large cardinals in the region of
I_{0}
(see
[
5
, Theorem 65]
).

The technical content of the manuscript

1. The Largest Suslin Axiom

{\sf{LSA}}
is a determinacy theory whose underlying theory is Woodin’s
\sf{AD}^{+}
. Chapter 9.1 of
[
70
]
provides a quick overview of
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
, and Larson’s recent manuscript
[
19
]
provides more details. Perhaps the most important consequence of
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
is the fact that assuming
V=L({\wp}({\mathbb{R}}))
, the fragment of
V
coded by the Suslin, co-Suslin sets of reals is
\Sigma_{1}
elementary in
V
(see Theorem 9.7 of
[
70
]
).

We will need the following concepts to introduce
{\sf{LSA}}
. A cardinal
\kappa
is
\sf{OD}
-inaccessible if for every
\alpha<\kappa
there is no surjection
f:{\wp}(\alpha)\rightarrow\kappa
that is definable from ordinal parameters. A set of reals
A\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}
is
\kappa
-
Suslin
if for some tree
T
on
\kappa
,
A=p[T]
2
2

2

Given a cardinal
\kappa
, we say
T\subseteq\bigcup_{n<\omega}\omega^{n}\times\kappa^{n}
is a
tree
on
\kappa
if
T
is closed under initial segments. Given a tree
T
on
\kappa
, we let
[T]
be the set of its branches, i.e.,
b\in[T]
if
b\in\omega^{\omega}\times\kappa^{\omega}
and letting
b=(b_{0},b_{1})
, for each
n\in\omega
,
(b_{0}\restriction n,b_{1}\restriction n)\in T
. We then let
p[T]=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}:\exists f((x,f)\in[T])\}
.
. A set
A
is
Suslin
if it is
\kappa
-Suslin for some
\kappa
;
A
is
co-Suslin
if its complement
\mathbb{R}\backslash A
is Suslin. A set
A
is
Suslin, co-Suslin
if both
A
and its complement are Suslin. A cardinal
\kappa
is a
Suslin cardinal
if there is a set of reals
A
such that
A
is
\kappa
-Suslin but
A
is not
\lambda
-Suslin for any
\lambda<\kappa
. Suslin cardinals play an important role in the study of models of determinacy as can be seen by just flipping through the Cabal Seminar Volumes (
[
17
]
,
[
14
]
,
[
15
]
,
[
16
]
).
\sf{LSA}
is then the following theory.

Definition 1.0.1
.

The
\sf{Largest\ Suslin\ Axiom}
, abbreviated as
\sf{LSA}
, is the conjunction of the following statements:

1.

{\sf{ZF}}+\sf{AD}^{+}
.

2.

There is a largest Suslin cardinal.

3.

The largest Suslin cardinal is
\sf{OD}
-inaccessible.

\hfill\dashv

\sf{LSA}
can also be defined in terms of the
Solovay sequence
.

Definition 1.0.2
.

The Solovay sequence is a sequence
(\theta_{\alpha}:\alpha\leq\Omega)
such that

1.

\theta_{0}=\sup\{\beta:\exists f:{\wp}(\omega)\rightarrow\beta(f
is an
OD
surjection
)\}
,

2.

if
\theta_{\alpha}<\Theta
then
\theta_{\alpha+1}=\sup\{\beta:\exists f:{\wp}(\theta_{\alpha})\rightarrow\beta(f
is an
OD
surjection
)\}
,

3.

for limit
\lambda\leq\Omega
,
\theta_{\lambda}=\sup_{\alpha<\lambda}\theta_{\alpha}
.

4.

\theta_{\Omega}=\Theta
.

\hfill\dashv

Remark 1.0.3
.

\sf{LSA}
is then equivalent to the conjunction of the following axioms:

1.

{\sf{ZF}}+\sf{AD}^{+}
.

2.

For some ordinal
\alpha
,
\Theta=\theta_{\alpha+1}
and
\theta_{\alpha}
is the largest Suslin cardinal
<\Theta
.

\hfill\dashv

The above equivalence can be shown using the material of Chapter 9.1 of
[
70
]
. We note that it follows from
[
70
, Theorem 9.12]
that
\sf{LSA}
implies
\neg\sf{AD}_{{\mathbb{R}}}
.

2. The minimal model of LSA

Suppose
V
is a model of
{\sf{LSA}}
. Let
\kappa
be the largest Suslin cardinal and suppose
A\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}
has Wadge rank
\kappa
. It then follows that
L(A,{\mathbb{R}})\vDash{\sf{LSA}}
. Keeping this fact in mind, we make the following definition.

Definition 1.0.4
.

Suppose
T
is a first order theory extending
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
. We say that
M
is
a minimal model
of
T
if

•

M
is transitive and
M\vDash T
,

•

{\mathbb{R}},Ord\subseteq M
, and

•

for every
N
that is a (definable) class of
M
and contains all the reals and ordinals, either
N=M
or
N\vDash\neg{\sf{LSA}}
.

\hfill\dashv

It follows that all minimal models of
{\sf{LSA}}
have the form
L(A,{\mathbb{R}})
. A natural question is whether there is a unique minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
. We will show (see the proof of Theorem
10.3.1
) that in fact there is a unique minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
which is naturally
the
minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
. Woodin’s proof of the existence of divergent models of
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
also shows that not all extensions of
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
have a unique minimal model (see
[
7
, Theorem 6.1]
).

The minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
may not actually be big. For example, if
N
is a transitive model of
\sf{AD^{+}}
that contains the minimal model
M
of
{\sf{LSA}}
and has a Suslin cardinal
>\Theta^{M}
then
\Theta^{M}<\theta_{0}^{N}
. In particular, every set of reals in
M
is ordinal definable from a real in
N
. Motivated by this fact, we make the following definition.

Definition 1.0.5
.

Suppose
M
is a transitive model containing all the reals and ordinals and such that
M\vDash{\sf{AD^{+}}}+V=L({\wp}({\mathbb{R}}))
. We say
M
is
full
if for all transitive
N
such that

•

M\subseteq N
and

•

N\vDash``{\sf{AD^{+}}}+V=L({\wp}({\mathbb{R}}))
”,

\Theta^{M}
is a member of the Solovay sequence of
N
.
\hfill\dashv

The following interesting problem seems central to our understanding of the models of
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
that we build from large cardinals or from other hypothesis.

Problem 1.0.6
.

Do large cardinals or forcing axioms such as
{\sf{PFA}}
imply that there is a full model of
{\sf{LSA}}
?

In particular, whether the models of determinacy obtained as derived models of
V
contain full models of
{\sf{LSA}}
or not is a major open problem of the area.
Here we make the following conjecture which is motivated by Woodin’s
Sealing Theorem
(see
[
20
]
). Below
{\sf{uB}}
stands for the set of universally Baire sets and for a generic
g
,
{\sf{uB}}_{g}=({\sf{uB}})^{V[g]}
and
{\mathbb{R}}_{g}={\mathbb{R}}^{V[g]}
.

Conjecture 1.0.7
.

Suppose
\kappa
is a supercompact cardinal and there is a proper class of Woodin cardinals. Let
g\subseteq Coll(\omega,2^{2^{\kappa}})
be generic. Then in
L({\sf{uB}}_{g},{\mathbb{R}}_{g})
, for each
\xi<\Theta
there is
\alpha
such that
\theta_{\alpha}\in(\xi,\Theta)
and
\theta_{\alpha}
is the largest Suslin cardinal below
\theta_{\alpha+1}
.

Thus, in the set up of the conjecture,
L({\sf{uB}}_{g},{\mathbb{R}}_{g})
has full models of
{\sf{LSA}}
that are cofinal in its Wadge hierarchy. The following is what is known on Conjecture
1.0.7
. Woodin (unpublished) has shown that
L({\sf{uB}}_{g},{\mathbb{R}}_{g})\vDash``{\sf{AD}}_{\mathbb{R}}+\Theta
is a regular cardinal”. Sandra Müller and the first author recently showed that
L({\sf{uB}}_{g},{\mathbb{R}}_{g})
can be represented as a derived model of some iterate of
V
. They also found a stationary-tower-free proof of Woodin’s Sealing Theorem. These results are unpublished.
[
57
]
presents a stationary-tower-free proof of the derived model theorem.

The question of whether the Cramer-Woodin model of
{\sf{LSA}}
from
[
5
, Theorem 65]
is a full model of
{\sf{LSA}}
or not seems not only interesting but also important for understanding the relationship between large cardinals and models of
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
.

3. The content of this manuscript

In this manuscript, we establish three kinds of results that can be stated without mentioning the technology developed to prove them. The first set of results deals with the minimal model of
\sf{LSA}
. Assume
V
is the minimal model of
\sf{LSA}
. Then the following holds.

(A) (Theorem
7.2.2
)
{\rm{HOD}}\vDash\sf{GCH}
.

(B) (Theorem
10.2.1
) The Mouse Set Conjecture holds.

The second set of results contains a single result which shows the consistency of
\sf{LSA}
relative to large cardinals. We will show the following.

(C) (Corollary
10.3.1
) Suppose the theory
\sf{ZFC}+``
there is a Woodin cardinal that is a limit of Woodin cardinals” is consistent. Then so is
\sf{LSA}
.

The third type of result establishes the existence of the minimal model of
\sf{LSA}
assuming combinatorial principles or forcing axioms. The following belongs to this group.

(D) (Corollary
12.0.3
) Assume
\sf{PFA}
. Then the minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
exists.

The precursors of these results already exist in print. The first author demonstrated versions of (A), (B), and (C) for the theory
\sf{AD}_{\mathbb{R}}+``\Theta
is a regular cardinal”. The second author proved the version of (D) for the same theory. The interested reader may consult
[
30
]
,
[
32
]
and
[
67
]
. The reason to prove such results is to demonstrate that the underlying technical theory is robust and can be used in a wide range of situations.

Recently the authors of
[
2
]
showed that the theory
{\sf{CH}}+``
there is an
\omega_{1}
-dense ideal on
\omega_{1}
” implies that the minimal model of
{\sf{AD}}_{{\mathbb{R}}}+``\Theta
is a regular cardinal” exists. This, along with an earlier result of Woodin, show that these two theories are equiconsistent. This solved part of Problem 12 of
[
70
]
. Whether there is a natural hypothesis asserting the existence of an ideal on a small cardinal that is equiconsistent with
{\sf{LSA}}
is an interesting problem. In particular, letting
M^{\prime}
be the minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
,
\kappa
be the largest Suslin cardinal of
M^{\prime}
and
M=L(\Gamma,{\mathbb{R}})
where
\Gamma=\{A\in{\wp}({\mathbb{R}})\cap M^{\prime}:w(A)<\kappa\}
3
3

3

w(A)
is the Wadge rank of
A
.
, the model
M[G*H]
where
G*H\subseteq Coll(\omega_{1},{\mathbb{R}})*Add(1,\omega_{2})
is
M
-generic has not be studied at all. The model
M[G*H]
where
G*H\subseteq\mathbb{P}_{max}*Add(1,\omega_{3})

[

4

4

But see also

4. The necessity of the short-tree-strategy mice

We do not know how to prove (B)-(D) using the methods of
[
65
]
, and whether this is possible or not is a very interesting question
5
5

5

[
65
]
does show that
{\mathcal{H}}\vDash{\sf{GCH}}
but only assuming
{\sf{HPC}}
.
. The main issue seems to be the absence of an analysis of the
{\sf{LSA}}
stages of the Solovay sequence using the least-branch hierarchy. The main technical concept we use to analyze such levels is the notion of a
short-tree-strategy mice
, which is developed in Chapter
3
. Thus, the question is whether it is necessary to develop this theory in order to prove results like (B)-(D).

The main issue is the following. Assume
{\sf{AD}^{+}}
. Suppose
\theta_{\alpha+1}<\Theta
and
\theta_{\alpha}
is the largest Suslin cardinal below
\theta_{\alpha+1}
. Then if
({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
is the hod pair generating the pointclass
\Gamma_{1}=\{A\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}:w(A)<\theta_{\alpha+1}\}
then letting
\delta
be the largest Woodin cardinal of
{\mathcal{P}}
,
(({\mathcal{P}}|\delta)^{\#},\Sigma^{stc})
is the pair generating the pointclass
\Gamma_{0}=\{A\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}:w(A)<\theta_{\alpha}\}
. If one’s goal is to show that assuming
{\sf{AD}_{\mathbb{R}}}+{\sf{DC}}+V=L({\wp}({\mathbb{R}}))
,
{\rm{HOD}}\vDash{\sf{GCH}}
then it maybe possible to
skip

\Gamma_{0}
and build the generator of
\Gamma_{1}
. The problem with skipping
\Gamma_{0}
and moving to
\Gamma_{1}
is exactly the fact that it is then unclear how to prove theorems like (A)-(D). What one would have liked is some sort of hybrid method that doesn’t skip
\Gamma_{0}
but also incorporates ideas from
[
65
]
to avoid the theory of short-tree-strategy mice. It seems to us that this may not be possible.

Suppose then we decide not to skip over
\Gamma_{0}
, and suppose we have succeeded in building a generator
(({\mathcal{P}}|\delta)^{\#},\Sigma^{stc})
for
\Gamma_{0}
. At this stage, we do not know what
({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
must be and can only see
(({\mathcal{P}}|\delta)^{\#},\Sigma^{stc})
. Set then
{\mathcal{Q}}=({\mathcal{P}}|\delta)^{\#}
and
\Lambda=\Sigma^{stc}
. What we need to show next is that we can extend
{\mathcal{Q}}
to
{\mathcal{P}}
in such a way that the following hold
6
6

6

Below
H_{\delta}^{\mathcal{P}}
is the set of all
X\in{\mathcal{P}}
whose hereditary cardinality is
<\delta
.
:

1.

\delta
is the largest cardinal of
{\mathcal{P}}
and
H_{\delta}^{\mathcal{P}}={\mathcal{Q}}|\delta
,

2.

for all
A\subseteq\delta
,
A\in{\mathcal{P}}
if and only if
A
is ordinal definable from
({\mathcal{Q}},\Lambda)
,

3.

{\mathcal{P}}\vDash``\delta
is a Woodin cardinal”.

The main issue seems to be with proving clause 2. It is a version of
\sf{MSC}
for
\Lambda
, and the only way we know how to prove it is by building a
\Lambda
-mouse over
{\mathcal{Q}}
whose derived model contains the set
\{(x,y)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}:x
is ordinal definable from
y
and
({\mathcal{Q}},\Lambda)\}
. This requires a certain level of uniformity:
{\mathcal{Q}}
and what we build on the top of
{\mathcal{Q}}
have to be the same kind of objects, as otherwise the construction over
{\mathcal{Q}}
can project across
\delta
violating clause 3 above.

5. Some historical remarks on the large cardinal structure of hod mice

The large cardinal structure of hod mice has been somewhat of a mystery. While originally it seemed hod mice must have very limited large cardinal structure, nowadays the prevailing belief is that they in fact can have any large cardinal whatsoever
7
7

7

At least in the short-extender region.
. First we make the following definition.

Definition 1.0.8
.

\Theta_{reg}
is the theory
{\sf{ZF}}+{\sf{AD}}_{\mathbb{R}}+``\Theta
is a regular cardinal”.
\hfill\dashv

Prior to
[
30
]
, the theory
\Theta_{reg}
was believed to be beyond the short extender region and was believed to be at the complexity level of supercompact cardinals. Because Woodin was able to force strong combinatorial statements over a model of
\Theta_{reg}
that would normally require large cardinals at the level of supercompact cardinals or beyond
8
8

8

E.g.,
{\sf{MM^{++}}}(c)
(see
[
70
]
) and
{\sf{CH}}+``
there is an
\omega_{1}
-dense ideal on
\omega_{1}
” (see
[
2
]
).
, the aforementioned belief seemed to be very reasonable.

The main goal of
[
30
]
, which is based on the first author’s PhD thesis, was to analyze
{\rm{HOD}}
of the minimal model of
\Theta_{reg}
9
9

9

Prior
[
30
]
, it was not know that there is a unique minimal model of
\Theta_{reg}
.
. While any model of determinacy has a rich large cardinal structure below its
\Theta
10
10

10

E.g.,
\Theta
is a limit of strong partition cardinals, see
[
13
]
.
,
V_{\Theta}^{\rm{HOD}}
of the minimal model of
\Theta_{reg}
is very simple in the following sense (see Theorem
1.0.9
).

Suppose
V\vDash{\sf{AD^{+}}}
. The Solovay pointclasses are exactly the stages of the Wadge hierarchy where a “new”
non-definable from below
set appears. For
\alpha
such that
\theta_{\alpha}\leq\Theta
let
{\sf{SP}}_{\alpha}=\{B\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}:w(B)<\theta_{\alpha}\}
. If
\theta_{\alpha}<\Theta
and
A\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}
has Wadge rank
\theta_{\alpha}
then
A
is not ordinal definable from any set of reals
B\in{\sf{SP}}_{\alpha}
and moreover, every set in
{\sf{SP}}_{\alpha+1}
is ordinal definable from
A
and a real. Thus, in a sense, once we perceive a set of reals of Wadge rank
\theta_{\alpha}
, we know everything about
{\sf{SP}}_{\alpha+1}
. Putting it differently,

\dagger:
in the Wadge hierarchy, nothing of any interest happens among sets whose Wadge rank belongs to the interval
(\theta_{\alpha},\theta_{\alpha+1})
.

In general,
\dagger
is not true. All sorts of structures: Suslin cardinals, large cardinals with complicated partition properties etc, exist in that Wadge interval. However, the hod mice that are below the theory
\Theta_{reg}
cannot have regular limits of Woodin cardinals, and moreover, the Woodin cardinals and their limits of such a hod mouse exactly correspond to the Solovay sequence
11
11

11

By a theorem of Woodin, each
\theta_{\alpha+1}
is a Woodin cardinal of
{\rm{HOD}}
. See
[
18
]
.
in the following sense.

Theorem 1.0.9
(
[
30
]
and Theorem
7.2.2
).

In the minimal model of
\Theta_{reg}
, and in fact of
\sf{LSA}
,
\delta
is a Woodin cardinal of
{\rm{HOD}}
or a limit of Woodin cardinals of
{\rm{HOD}}
if and only if
\delta
is a member of the Solovay sequence.

Theorem
1.0.9
implies that
{\rm{HOD}}
of the minimal model of
\Theta_{reg}
has no Woodin cardinals in the interval
(\theta_{\alpha},\theta_{\alpha+1})
, and in this sense,
\dagger
is true below
\Theta_{reg}
12
12

12

It is a well-known fact from inner model theory dating back to
[
22
]
that iteration strategies of mice or hod mice acquire complexity only because of Woodin cardinals.
. Therefore, to represent
V_{\Theta}^{\rm{HOD}}
of the minimal model of
\Theta_{reg}
as a hod mouse, we do not need to understand exactly what happens between
(\theta_{\alpha},\theta_{\alpha+1})
in
V
as none of what happens there makes
{\rm{HOD}}
look complicated in that interval
13
13

13

This was the original motivation of the so-called “layering” used both in
[
30
]
and in this manuscript.
.

The world of determinacy might have been a simpler place if
\dagger
was always true, but
[
30
]
shows that the theory
\Theta_{reg}
is much weaker than a Woodin cardinal that is a limit of Woodin cardinals.
\sf{LSA}
, the main topic of this manuscript, is the next natural determinacy theory that is consistency wise stronger than
\Theta_{reg}
, and while the hod mice of this manuscript do have inaccessible limit of Woodin cardinals, Theorem
1.0.9
is still true. This once again implies that the large cardinal structure of hod mice at the level of
{\sf{LSA}}
is limited and in fact, in such hod mice

(
\ddagger
) there is no Woodin cardinal
\delta
and a
\kappa<\delta
such that
\kappa
is
\delta
-strong.

Moreover, prior to the current work, it was believed that
\ddagger
and Theorem
1.0.9
are just consequences of
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
. This belief was based on various arguments due to Woodin that showed that if
\delta
is a member of the Solovay sequence then there cannot be
\kappa<\delta
whose Mitchell order was much bigger than
\delta
. However, Theorem
10.3.1
shows that
{\sf{LSA}}
is weaker than a Woodin cardinal that is a limit of Woodin cardinals, and further unpublished work of the first author showed that the large cardinal structure of hod mice, at least in the short extender region, may not be limited. In particular, neither
\dagger
nor Theorem
1.0.9
are consequences of
{\sf{AD}}^{+}
. The first author then made the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.0.10
.

Assume
{\sf{AD^{+}}}+V=L({\wp}({\mathbb{R}}))
. Define the sequence
(\eta_{\alpha}:\alpha\leq\Omega)
as follows:

1.

3.

For a limit ordinal

Then

Using the methods of

6. Organization.

Chapters 2-8 develop the basic theory of hod mice for
\sf{AD}^{+}
models up to the minimal model of
\sf{LSA}
; a consequence of this analysis is (A). The last four chapters focus on applications. Chapter
11
proves that
\square_{\kappa,2}
holds in HOD of
\sf{AD}^{+}
models up to the minimal model of
\sf{LSA}
for all HOD-cardinals
\kappa
. Our main use of this chapter is Chapter
12
, where a proof of (D) is given. Chapter
9
develops the basic theory of
condensing sets
, which is needed in constructions of hod mice in various situations. Chapter
10
uses the material developed in the previous chapters to prove (B) and (C). The last chapter (Chapter 12) proves (D) by constructing a hybrid version of
K^{c}
. This chapter uses methods developed in the previous chapters,
[
37
]
, and
[
67
]
.

Definition 2.3.1

We say

.

Notice that if

f
.

Jumping ahead, we remark that iteration strategies and mouse operators provide an ample source of amenable functions. For instance, let
{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{M}}_{1}^{\#}
and let
\Sigma
be its canonical iteration strategy. We define
f
as follows. Let first
{\rm dom}(f)
be the set of structures of the form
w=(\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}^{w}),{\mathcal{T}}^{w},\in)
where
{\mathcal{T}}^{w}
12
12

12

One could think of
{\mathcal{T}}
as a sequence
({\mathcal{T}}\restriction\alpha:\alpha<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}}))
.
is a normal iteration tree on
{\mathcal{M}}
of limit length and is according to
\Sigma
. Next, define
f(w)=b
where
b=\Sigma({\mathcal{T}}^{w})
. Then
f
is amenable. We will refer to such an
f
as
an amenable function given by an iteration strategy
.

The definitions that follow explain how our indexing schemes work. We first isolate those iterations whose branches will be indexed. The reader may think of the formula
\phi
appearing in Notation
2.3.2
as the formula that defines the set of iterations whose branches need to be indexed. However,
\phi
alone does not define such iterations as we need to add clause 2 for technical reasons. The ordinal
\beta
essentially identifies the location where the branch of the iteration tree defined by
\phi
should be indexed.

In general, to develop a reasonable theory of hybrid
\mathcal{J}
-structures, we need to use indexing schemes to index branches of stacks. The reason for this is that if no particular coherent method of indexing is used to organize such structures then one cannot in general hope to develop a comparison theory for the resulting structures. Indeed, if
{\mathcal{M}}
and
{\mathcal{N}}
are unindexed hybrid
\mathcal{J}
-structures then it is possible that some
b
is indexed at
\alpha
in
{\mathcal{M}}
but nothing is indexed at
\alpha
in
{\mathcal{N}}
, causing a fatal breakdown of the comparison argument. Nevertheless, in Section
3.8
, it will be convenient to work with unindexed hybrid
\mathcal{J}
-structures (as defined in Definition
2.5.3
).

Another important remark is that it might be convenient to think of the indexing scheme as a parameter of the hybrid
\mathcal{J}
-structures, in the same way we internalize the fine structural parameter. Thus, instead of
{\mathcal{M}}
we could consider
({\mathcal{M}},\phi)
where
\phi
is the indexing scheme. However, in most cases, isolating
\phi
won’t matter so much, and so we will not take this path.
We suspect that
{\mathcal{M}}
may even recognize many different
\phi
s as its own indexing scheme
13
13

13

Of course, this can be achieved trivially;
\phi
and
0=0\wedge\phi
are equivalent. But there could be two different indexing schemes
\phi
and
\phi^{\prime}
such that
{\sf{ZFC}}
or any natural extension of it, does not prove
\phi\mathrel{\leftrightarrow}\phi^{\prime}
yet there is
{\mathcal{M}}
which is both
\phi
indexed and
\phi^{\prime}
-indexed.
. Thus we may have two
\phi
-indexed
{\mathcal{M}}
and
{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}
and an indexing scheme
\phi^{\prime}
such that
{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}
is
\phi^{\prime}
-indexed while
{\mathcal{M}}
is not. However, such issues will not come up in the sequel.

Remark 2.3.4
(The measurable cofinality issue).

The reader unfamiliar with

strategic mice may find clause 2 of Definition
2.3.8
somewhat odd. This clause has to do with an issue known to experts and was first discovered in earlier versions of
[
41
]
15
15

15

The authors were unable to locate the discussion involving the measurable cofinality issue in
[
41
]
.
. The problem was fully treated in
[
50
]
, and the discussion appears in
[
50
, Remark 2.47]
. Without getting too much into the technical details, the issue is simply that if
{\mathcal{M}}=\mathcal{J}^{A,f}
is a
{\mathcal{J}}
-structure such that the
f
predicate codes a strategy for some
{\mathcal{N}}\in{\mathcal{M}}
,
w=_{def}({\mathcal{J}}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}),{\mathcal{T}},\in)\in{\rm dom}(f)
,
\kappa=_{def}{\rm cf}^{\mathcal{M}}({\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}}))
is a measurable cardinal in
{\mathcal{M}}
,
f(w)
is indexed at
\lambda
and
E\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}}
is an extender with
{\rm crit}(E)=\kappa
then

\sup(\pi^{{\mathcal{M}}||(\lambda,0)}_{E}[{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})])<\pi_{E}({\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}}))
while
\lambda={\rm ord}(Ult({\mathcal{M}}||(\lambda,0),E))
.

The issue is hiding in the fact that in most of the natural attempts to organize strategic mice,
{\rm cf}^{\mathcal{M}}(\lambda)=\kappa
, while in the above situation this fails in
Ult({\mathcal{M}}||(\lambda,0),E)
for
\pi_{E}^{{\mathcal{M}}||(\lambda,0)}({\mathcal{T}})
.
\hfill\dashv

Remark 2.3.9
.

Definition
2.3.8
leaves open one important question. Does it follow that
S^{\mathcal{M}}_{\phi}={\rm dom}(f^{\mathcal{M}})
? The answer is of course that none of the conditions we have imposed on
f^{\mathcal{M}}
guarantees that
S^{\mathcal{M}}_{\phi}={\rm dom}(f^{\mathcal{M}})
. It could be that some
w\in S^{\mathcal{M}}_{\phi}
but it is not
(f,\phi)
-minimal. However, if
f^{\mathcal{M}}
is supposed to code an iteration strategy
\Sigma
of some
P
then the fact that
w\in S^{\mathcal{M}}_{\phi}
implies that
w
is an iteration according to
\Sigma
and that we must have that
w\in{\rm dom}(f^{\mathcal{M}})
. What will in fact happen, in intuitive terms, is that while
w
may not be in
{\rm dom}(f^{\mathcal{M}})
, it will be in
{\rm dom}(f^{\mathcal{N}})
for some
{\mathcal{N}}
extending
{\mathcal{M}}
. This may not be possible to arrange if for example
{\mathcal{N}}=_{def}{\mathcal{J}}_{\omega}({\mathcal{M}})
projects in a way that say
w
is no longer in
{\sf{core}}_{1}({\mathcal{N}})
, but if
{\mathcal{M}}
is the final model of some reasonable fully backgrounded construction that produces hybrid premouse then we will indeed have that
S^{\mathcal{M}}_{\phi}={\rm dom}(f^{\mathcal{M}})
. This is because it can be shown that any
w\in S^{\mathcal{M}}_{\phi}
is
(f,\phi)
-minimal.

To see this in intuitive terms, suppose towards a contradiction that some
w\in S^{\mathcal{M}}_{\phi}
doesn’t belong to
{\rm dom}(f^{\mathcal{M}})
. We can assume
w
is
<_{\mathcal{M}}
-minimal. Now, and this depends on our choice of
\phi
, the indexing scheme
\phi
will be
\Sigma_{1}
and hence, it will have the following upward absoluteness property: if for some
\nu
,
{\mathcal{M}}|\nu\vDash\phi[w]
then for all
\nu^{\prime}\geq\nu
,
{\mathcal{M}}|\nu^{\prime}\vDash\phi[w]
. Let
\xi<{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}})
be such that whenever
u\in S^{\mathcal{M}}_{\phi}
and
u<_{{\mathcal{M}}}w
then
\sup(f(u))<\xi
. Such
\xi
will exist because, in concrete applications,
{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}})
will be a Woodin cardinal of the universe. It follows that to show that
w\in{\rm dom}(f^{\mathcal{M}})
it is enough to show that there is
\beta\in(\xi,{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}}))
such that
{\mathcal{M}}|\beta\vDash{\rm{ZFC}}
. Since
{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}})
is a Woodin cardinal of the background universe, there are plenty of such
\beta
.
\hfill\dashv

-indexed layered hybrid
\mathcal{J}
-structure over a self-well-ordered set
X
and
\vec{E}
is a sequence of extenders. We say
\eta
is a cutpoint of
{\mathcal{M}}
if there is no
\alpha\in{\rm dom}(\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}})
such that
{\rm crit}(\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}}(\alpha))<\eta\leq\alpha
. We say
\vec{E}
is a
mixed indexed extender sequence
if the following clauses hold:

1.

(j-like indexing) If
\kappa={\rm crit}(E)
is a limit of Woodin cardinals of
{\mathcal{M}}
and is a cutpoint of
{\mathcal{M}}
then letting
{\mathcal{N}}=\pi^{\mathcal{M}}_{E}({\mathcal{M}}|(\kappa^{+})^{\mathcal{M}})
,
E
is indexed at
(\eta^{+})^{\mathcal{N}}
where
\eta=\sup\{\alpha\in{\rm dom}(\vec{E}^{{\mathcal{N}}}):{\rm crit}(\vec{E}^{\mathcal{N}}(\alpha))=\kappa\}
.

2.

(ms-indexing) All other extenders are indexed according to the ms-indexing.

The initial segment condition for
E
is clause 3 of
[
60
, Definition 2.4]
.
There are many papers in the literature that connect the two indexing schemes. For example, the reader may consult
[
8
]
,
[
9
]
, and
[
46
]
. Our goal in this book is to present the theory of the minimal model of the Largest Suslin Axiom in as shorter space as we can, and because of this we will avoid fine structural issues that have been well-treated in the literature.

Definition 2.3.14
(Layered hybrid e-structure).

Suppose
{\mathcal{M}}=\mathcal{J}^{\vec{E},f}(X)
is a
\phi
-indexed layered hybrid
\mathcal{J}
-structure over a self-well-ordered set
X
.
{\mathcal{M}}
is called a
\phi
-indexed layered hybrid potential e-structure
(
\sf{lhpes}
) if
\vec{E}
is a mixed indexed extender sequence. We write
\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}}
for
\vec{E}
etc.

If
{\mathcal{M}}
is an
\sf{lhpes}
and
E=\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}}(\gamma)
then we let
{\rm ind}^{\mathcal{M}}(E)=\gamma
.

We say that
{\mathcal{M}}
is a
\phi
-indexed layered hybrid e-structure (
\sf{lhes}
) if
{\mathcal{M}}=({\mathcal{M}}^{\prime},k)
is an f.s.
{\mathcal{J}}
-structure such that
{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}
is a
\phi
-indexed
\sf{lhpes}
and for every

,
{\mathcal{M}}||(\omega\beta,m)
is sound.
\hfill\dashv

Mixed indexing smoothens implementation of certain technical arguments. The most crucial property for us is the following. Suppose
E
is an extender on the extender sequence of an
\sf{lhes}

{\mathcal{M}}
such that
{\mathcal{M}}\vDash``{\rm crit}(E)
is a cutpoint and a limit of Woodin cardinals” (i.e. there is no
F\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}}
such that
{\rm crit}(F)<{\rm crit}(E)\leq{\rm ind}^{\mathcal{M}}(F)
). So
E
has j-like indexing. Let
\gamma=\sup\{\xi:\xi<{\rm ind}^{\mathcal{M}}(E),\xi\in{\rm dom}(\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}})
and
{\rm crit}(E_{\xi})={\rm crit}(E)\}
. Then
\gamma=\sup\{\xi:\xi\in{\rm dom}(\vec{E}^{Ult({\mathcal{M}},E)})
and
{\rm crit}(E_{\xi})={\rm crit}(E)\}
. The advantage of mixed indexing over other indexing schemes can be seen in Definition
2.8
.

For an
\sf{lhes}

{\mathcal{M}}
with just one layer (that is,
|Y^{\mathcal{M}}|=1
), we say
{\mathcal{M}}
is a
hybrid e-structure
(
\sf{hes}
). Next we introduce
\sf{lhes}
that are internally closed under sharps. We will use such a closure to introduce short tree strategy premice (see Definition
2.5.2
and Definition
3.8.17
).

Definition 2.3.15
(Closed
\sf{lhes}
).

Suppose
{\mathcal{M}}
is an
\sf{lhes}
and
\alpha\leq{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}})
. Then we say
{\mathcal{M}}
is
closed
below
\alpha
if for all
\beta<\alpha
there is
\gamma\in{\rm dom}(\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}})
such that
\gamma<\alpha
and
{\rm crit}(E_{\gamma}^{\mathcal{M}})>\beta
. We say
{\mathcal{M}}
is closed if
{\mathcal{M}}
is closed below
{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}})
.
\hfill\dashv

2.4

Below we review iteration trees. Our notation is mostly in line with most of the references we have quoted above in Section

\sf{lhes}

Remark 2.4.7
(Semi-smooth convention).

Because we will mostly work with semi-smooth stacks on

Strategies.

Given a stack
{\mathcal{T}}

{\mathcal{W}}_{\geq{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})}={\mathcal{U}}

35

35

After obvious re-enumeration of its members.
. We may often say that

is a normal iteration tree if after straightforward re-enumeration of its members it becomes a normal iteration tree.

36

36

In this re-enumeration we must set

Suppose
{\mathcal{M}}
is an
\sf{lhes}
and
\Sigma
is a function. We say
\Sigma
is an iteration strategy for
{\mathcal{M}}
if whenever

{\mathcal{T}}
is a stack on
{\mathcal{M}}

is a cofinal well-founded branch of
{\mathcal{T}}
.

A putative iteration tree
{\mathcal{T}}
on
{\mathcal{M}}
is according to
\Sigma
if for all limit ordinals
\alpha<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})

{\mathcal{T}}_{<\alpha}\in{\rm dom}(\Sigma)
and
\Sigma({\mathcal{T}}_{<\alpha})=[0,\alpha)_{\mathcal{T}}
. We say
\Sigma
is a
\kappa
-strategy for
{\mathcal{M}}
if

1.

\Sigma
is an iteration strategy for
{\mathcal{M}}
such that if
{\mathcal{T}}\in{\rm dom}(\Sigma)
then
{\mathcal{T}}
is a normal iteration tree on
{\mathcal{M}}
of length

,

2.

if
{\mathcal{T}}
is a normal iteration tree on
{\mathcal{M}}
such that
{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})<\kappa
,
{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
is a limit ordinal and
{\mathcal{T}}
is according to
\Sigma
then
{\mathcal{T}}\in{\rm dom}(\Sigma)
,

3.

if
{\mathcal{T}}\in{\rm dom}(\Sigma)
,
b=\Sigma({\mathcal{T}})
and
{\mathcal{U}}
is a normal finite putative iteration tree on
{\mathcal{M}}^{\mathcal{T}}_{b}
such that
{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})+{\rm lh}({\mathcal{U}})<\kappa
and
{\mathcal{T}}^{\frown}{\mathcal{U}}
is a normal putative iteration tree on
{\mathcal{M}}
(after obvious re-enumeration of it) then
{\mathcal{U}}
is an iteration tree.

Alternatively,
\Sigma
is a
\kappa
-strategy if it is a winning strategy for II in the iteration game
\mathcal{G}({\mathcal{M}},\kappa)
. This game is defined immediately after
[
60
, Definition 3.3]
. The subscript
k
that appears in this game is just

.

Similarly we can define
(\kappa,\lambda)
-strategy for
{\mathcal{M}}
that acts on stacks. Here
\kappa
bounds the number of normal components and
\lambda
bounds the length of the normal components of the stacks. The relevant iteration game,
\mathcal{G}({\mathcal{M}},\kappa,\lambda)
appears soon after
[
60
, Remark 4.3]
.

The common part.

Given a normal iteration tree
{\mathcal{T}}
we let the common part of
{\mathcal{T}}
be

{\rm m}({\mathcal{T}})=\cup_{\alpha<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})}{\mathcal{M}}^{\mathcal{T}}_{\alpha}|{\rm ind}_{\alpha}^{\mathcal{T}}
.

Usually in literature, for example in
[
60
]
,
{\rm m}({\mathcal{T}})
is denoted by
{\mathcal{M}}({\mathcal{T}})
. However, inner model theorists make
{\mathcal{M}}
tired, and so in this book we give it less weight to carry than its usual heavy load. Following
[
60
]
we let
\delta({\mathcal{T}})={\rm ord}({\rm m}({\mathcal{T}}))=\sup\{{\rm ind}^{\mathcal{T}}_{\alpha}:\alpha<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})\}
.

2.5
Layered strategy e-structures

In this manuscript, we are mostly concerned with
\sf{lhes}
whose
f
predicate codes a strategy. The goal of this section is to introduce the language used to describe such structures.

Suppose that
{\mathcal{M}}
is an
\sf{lhes}
. We then say that a shifted amenable function
f

codes a partial strategy function
for
{\mathcal{M}}
if letting
g
be the amenable component of
f
, the following conditions hold:

1.

{\rm dom}(f)\subseteq\{(\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}),{\mathcal{T}},\in):{\mathcal{T}}
is a stack on
{\mathcal{M}}
without a last model
\}
.

2.

Whenever
{\mathcal{T}}
is a stack on
{\mathcal{M}}
such that
(\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}),{\mathcal{T}},\in)\in{\rm dom}(f)
and whenever
{\mathcal{U}}
is an initial segment of
{\mathcal{T}}
without a last model,
(\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{U}}),{\mathcal{U}},\in)\in{\rm dom}(f)
and

g((\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{U}}),{\mathcal{U}},\in))=[0,{\rm lh}({\mathcal{U}}))_{\mathcal{T}}
.

3.

For all
(\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}),{\mathcal{T}},\in)\in{\rm dom}(f)
,
g((\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}),{\mathcal{T}},\in))
is a cofinal branch of
{\mathcal{T}}
.

Notice that we do not require that

(a)
g((\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}),{\mathcal{T}},\in))
is a well-founded branch of
{\mathcal{T}}
,

(b) if
(\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}),{\mathcal{T}},\in)\in{\rm dom}(f)
and
b=g((\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}),{\mathcal{T}},\in))
is a cofinal well-founded branch of
{\mathcal{T}}
then any reasonable finite extension of
{\mathcal{T}}^{\frown}\{b\}
has well-founded models.

Conditions (a) and (b) will be part of a more restrictive notion.

When defining short tree strategy mice, we will encounter hybrid structures whose
f
predicate doesn’t necessarily code a strategy but a partial strategy. We make this notion more precise. First we make a useful definition.

In most applications,

Remark 2.5.6
.

Unless indicated otherwise, we will always tacitly assume that the extenders used to witness the existence of large cardinals in
\sf{lses}
belong to the extender sequence of the
\sf{lses}
. Thus, when we say “
\kappa
is a measurable cardinal in
{\mathcal{M}}
” we mean that there is an extender
E\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{M}}
such that
E
witnesses that
\kappa
is a measurable cardinal in
{\mathcal{M}}
. In
[
51
]
, Schlutzenberg extensively studied the problem of whether in pure extender models all large cardinal properties are witnessed by extenders that are indexed on the extender sequence. In particular, he showed that measurability and Woodinness are witnessed by extenders that are on the extender sequence.
\hfill\dashv

Remark 2.7.6
.

Before we give the definition we make the following intuitive remarks. Suppose
{\mathcal{P}}
is a hod premouse, which are the objects that we eventually want to define (see Definition
3.10.2
).

1.

The philosophy behind “layering” is the desire to make maximal complexity jumps in the Wadge hierarchy. Ordinary mice and premice are designed to reach large cardinals by using the least amount of information large cardinals give us, namely the extenders that induce those embeddings that we use to define the large cardinal in question. For example, to reach a measurable cardinal in a mouse we only use ultrafilters. However, measurability tells us much more than just that there is a nice ultrafilter on some cardinal. For example, if
\kappa
is measurable then every
\mathbb{\Pi}^{1}_{1}
set is
\kappa
-homogenously Suslin, and in trying to build mice with measurable cardinals we ignore this extra information. We justify our ignorance by claiming that our algorithms that produce mice (e.g. fully backgrounded constructions,
K^{c}
constructions and etc) using extenders as oracles output structures that do inherit all the important properties of large cardinals. That this indeed happens has been verified by Neeman for large cardinals in the region of Woodin cardinal that is a limit of Woodin cardinals (see
[
26
]
). However, a priori, this dream-like solution may have been wrong, and more of the information given to us by large cardinals might have been required to reach them in canonical structures, and perhaps the fact that we cannot do significantly better than a Woodin cardinal that is a limit of Woodin cardinals is a sign that only extenders won’t do.

Hod mice have an entirely different purpose. Instead of large cardinals the aim is to reach or rather “capture” the Wadge hierarchy inside canonical structures. This is parallel to Shoenfield’s Absoluteness, namely that
L
is
\Sigma^{1}_{2}
-correct. Each layer of a hod mouse corresponds to a new level of the Wadge hierarchy. However, what the philosophy of layering claims to be possible is that we can reach all levels of the Wadge hierarchy by simply jumping to the most significant levels of it, and here the significant levels of the Wadge hierarchy are defined to be
the Solovay pointclass
.

Definition 2.7.7
.

Assume
\sf{ZF+AD^{+}}
. We say
\Gamma
is a
Solovay pointclass
if there is
\kappa
such that
\kappa
is a member of the Solovy sequence and
\Gamma=\{A\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}:w(A)<\kappa\}
52
52

52

See Definition
1.0.2
.
.
\hfill\dashv

The strategy of each layer of a hod mouse generates a Solovay pointclass in the sense that the named strategy has Wadge rank
\theta_{\alpha}
for some
\alpha
. The dream of the “layering” philosophy is that by only generating the Solovay pointclasses we will reach all levels of the Wadge hierarchy. Internalizing this idea would help the reader with a knowledge of
{\sf{AD^{+}}}
theory to understand why layers are defined the way they are defined: every initial segment whose strategy corresponds to a Solovay pointclass is a layer.

Of course, at this stage the idea is vague. If
{\mathcal{P}}
is our hod mouse,
\Sigma
is an iteration strategy for
{\mathcal{P}}
,
{\mathcal{Q}}_{0}\triangleleft{\mathcal{Q}}_{1}\trianglelefteq{\mathcal{P}}
then the reader should expect that
\Sigma_{{\mathcal{Q}}_{0}}
is not more complex then
\Sigma_{{\mathcal{Q}}_{1}}
, and one can easily build many situations where in fact
\Sigma_{{\mathcal{Q}}_{0}}
is Wadge reducible to
\Sigma_{{\mathcal{Q}}_{1}}
but not vice a versa. However, it may be the case that neither
{\mathcal{Q}}_{0}
nor
{\mathcal{Q}}_{1}
are layers of
{\mathcal{P}}
. To make the idea work we need to
anticipate
the initial segments of
{\mathcal{P}}
whose strategies generate the Solovay pointclasses. Below we spell out what initial segments should be layers in the minimal model of
{\sf{LSA}}
.

2.

The basic phenomenon that guides us in our definition of layers is the following: Suppose
({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
is a pair such that
{\mathcal{P}}
is a hod mouse and
\Sigma
is its iteration strategy
53
53

53

For explanatory reasons, we are being somewhat vague.
. Let
{\mathcal{M}}_{\infty}({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
be the direct limit of all countable
\Sigma
-iterates of
{\mathcal{P}}
and
\pi_{{\mathcal{P}},\infty}:{\mathcal{P}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{M}}_{\infty}({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
be the direct limit embedding.

Key Phenomenon:
For
\delta\leq\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
,
\pi_{{\mathcal{P}},\infty}(\delta)
is a member of the Solovay sequence if and only if
\delta
is either a cutpoint Woodin cardinal of
{\mathcal{P}}
or a cutpoint limit of Woodin cardinals of
{\mathcal{P}}
.

The way we use the Key Phenomenon is as follows. Suppose we have declared
{\mathcal{Q}}
a layer of
{\mathcal{P}}
.

(a)

If
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
is a cutpoint Woodin cardinal of
{\mathcal{P}}
or a cutpoint limit of Woodin cardinals of
{\mathcal{P}}
then
{\mathcal{Q}}
is the unique layer
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
of
{\mathcal{P}}
such that
\delta^{{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}}=\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
.

(b)

If, however,
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}=o^{\mathcal{Q}}(\kappa)
for some
\kappa
and
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
is such that
\rho({\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime})\leq\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
then
\pi_{{\mathcal{Q}},\infty}(\kappa)\leq\pi_{{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime},\infty}(\kappa)
and the strict inequality cannot be ruled out. Thus, we declare
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
a layer as it can generate a new Solovay pointclass.

(c)

Also, suppose
\kappa<\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
is a limit of cutpoint Woodin cardinals of
{\mathcal{P}}
and suppose that
\alpha
is such that either
\alpha={\rm ind}^{\mathcal{P}}(E)
for some
E\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{P}}
with
{\rm crit}(E)=\kappa
or
\alpha
is a limit of such points. Notice now that for every
\beta<\alpha
,
\pi_{{\mathcal{P}}||(\omega\beta,\omega),\infty}(\kappa)<\pi_{{\mathcal{P}}||(\omega\alpha,\omega),\infty}(\kappa)
. This is because we must have that
\pi_{{\mathcal{P}}||(\omega\beta,\omega),\infty}=\pi_{Ult({\mathcal{P}},E)||(\omega\beta,\omega),\infty}
. Therefore,
{\mathcal{P}}||(\omega\alpha,\omega)
must be a layer of
{\mathcal{P}}
.

3.

Layers of
{\mathcal{P}}
are those proper initial segments of
{\mathcal{P}}
whose strategy is being indexed on the strategy predicate of
{\mathcal{P}}
, with the exception that
{\mathcal{P}}
is also considered to be a layer of itself.

4.

Meek layers of our hod mice were already studied in
[
30
]
.

5.

The key new ingredient of our hod mice is the way we treat the lsa type layers. Given an lsa type layer
{\mathcal{Q}}
of
{\mathcal{P}}
, say
{\mathcal{Q}}
is minimal in
{\mathcal{P}}
if there is no layer
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}\triangleleft{\mathcal{Q}}
such that
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}=\delta^{{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}}
. Given a minimal lsa type layer
{\mathcal{Q}}
, we start indexing the short-tree-strategy of
{\mathcal{Q}}
into the strategy predicate, and this leads to our notion of short-tree-strategy (
{\sf{sts}}
) premouse (see Definition
3.8.17
). There are two possibilities here. Either (a) we reach a level
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
with the property that
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
is an
{\sf{sts}}
premouse over
{\mathcal{Q}}
such that
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
is not a Woodin cardinal definably over
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
or (b)
\delta^{\mathcal{P}}=\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
,
\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
is Woodin in
{\mathcal{P}}
and
{\mathcal{P}}
above
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
is an
{\sf{sts}}
premouse. If we do reach such a
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
then
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
becomes a layer and we start adding the strategy of
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
. Notice that
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
itself is of lsa type.

6.

The following conditions essentially characterize all proper layers of
{\mathcal{P}}
, but the conditions below do not spell out the actual definition and are given for explanatory purposes.

(a)

(Woodin cardinals) If
\eta<\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
is a Woodin cardinal of
{\mathcal{P}}
then there is a layer
{\mathcal{Q}}
of
{\mathcal{P}}
such that
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}=\eta
.

(b)

(Limit of Woodin cardinals) If
\kappa<\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
is a limit of Woodin cardinals of
{\mathcal{P}}
then
{\mathcal{Q}}=_{def}{\mathcal{P}}|(\kappa^{+})^{\mathcal{P}}
is a layer of
{\mathcal{P}}
such that
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}=\kappa
and
{\mathcal{Q}}
is the unique layer
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
of
{\mathcal{P}}
with
\delta^{{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}}=\kappa
. Moreover,
\kappa
is a strong cutpoint in
{\mathcal{Q}}
(in particular, if
E\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{P}}
is such that
{\rm crit}(E)=\kappa
then
E
is total.)

(c)

(Active layers) If
\kappa<\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
is a limit of Woodin cardinals and
E\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{P}}
is such that
{\rm crit}(E)=\kappa
then there is a layer
{\mathcal{Q}}
of
{\mathcal{P}}
such that
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}={\rm ind}^{\mathcal{P}}(E)
.

(d)

(Limits of layers) If
\nu<\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
is a limit of ordinals of the form
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
where
{\mathcal{Q}}
is a layer of
{\mathcal{P}}
then there is a layer of
{\mathcal{P}}
such that
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}=\nu
.

(e)

If
{\mathcal{Q}}
is a layer of
{\mathcal{P}}
with
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}<\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
and
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}\trianglelefteq\mathcal{O}^{\mathcal{P}}_{{\rm ord}({\mathcal{Q}})}
is such that
\rho({\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime})\leq\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
then
{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}
is a layer of
{\mathcal{P}}
with
\delta^{{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime}}=\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
.

7.

The layers of a hod-like
\sf{lses}
are defined in a way that all non-meek layers are properly non-meek. There is no deep reason for doing this. The theory can be developed without this condition, but having more room above
\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
is a convenience.

\hfill\dashv

Remark 2.7.9
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{P}}
is an active
\sf{lses}
such that

1.

if
\alpha={\rm ord}({\mathcal{P}})
then
{\mathcal{P}}|\alpha
is a hod-like
\sf{lses}
,

2.

if
E=\vec{E}^{\mathcal{P}}(\alpha)
then
o^{{\mathcal{P}}|\alpha}({\rm crit}(E))=\delta^{{\mathcal{P}}|\alpha}
and

3.

\rho({\mathcal{P}})>{\rm crit}(E)
.

Then
{\mathcal{P}}
itself is hod-like. It falls under clause 2c of Definition
2.7.1
. Notice that
\alpha
is enumerated in the
\delta
-sequence of
{\mathcal{P}}
.
\hfill\dashv

Next we introduce hod-like
\sf{lses}
. These will eventually turn into hod premice. To do this we need to impose conditions on the layers of
\sf{lses}
, which are just the members of
Y^{\mathcal{P}}
where
{\mathcal{P}}
is an
{\sf{lses}}
.

Definition 2.7.10
(Hod-like
\sf{lses}
).

Suppose
{\mathcal{P}}
is a pre-hod-like
\sf{lses}
. We say
{\mathcal{P}}
is
hod-like
if the following conditions hold.

1.

\{{\mathcal{Q}}:{\mathcal{Q}}
is a proper layer of
{\mathcal{P}}\}=(Y^{\mathcal{P}}-X^{\mathcal{P}})
.

2.

For all layers
{\mathcal{Q}}
of
{\mathcal{P}}
such that
\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
is a limit of Woodin cardinals of
{\mathcal{P}}
,
{\rm ord}({\mathcal{Q}})
is a cardinal of
{\mathcal{P}}
.

\hfill\dashv

Remark 2.7.11
.

Perhaps clause 2 of Definition
2.7.10
needs some more explanation. According to Definition
2.7.8
if
\xi
is such that
{\mathcal{Q}}={\mathcal{Q}}_{\xi,0}
then

{\rm ord}({\mathcal{Q}})={\rm ord}(\mathcal{O}^{{\mathcal{P}}}_{\delta_{\xi}+1,{\mathcal{P}}|\delta_{\xi}})

which is the longest initial segment of
{\mathcal{P}}
whose strategy predicate codes a strategy for
{\mathcal{P}}|\delta_{\xi}={\mathcal{Q}}|\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
. A priori there is no reason for
{\rm ord}({\mathcal{Q}})
to be a cardinal. Clause 3, following
[
30
]
, makes this demand. It is a fullness condition that we will have to verify every time we build a hod premouse.
\hfill\dashv

Remark 2.7.12
.

Continuing with the set up of clause 2 of Definition
2.7.10
, it follows that if
E\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{P}}
is such that
{\rm crit}(E)=\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
then
E
is total. For if
E
is such that
{\rm crit}(E)=\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
then

\mathcal{O}^{\mathcal{P}}_{\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}+1,{\mathcal{P}}|\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}}\trianglelefteq{\mathcal{P}}|{\rm ind}^{\mathcal{P}}(E)
.

But if
E
is not total we must also have that
{\mathcal{P}}|{\rm ind}^{\mathcal{P}}(E)\trianglelefteq{\mathcal{P}}|((\delta^{\mathcal{Q}})^{+})^{\mathcal{P}}
.
\hfill\dashv

Remark 2.7.13
.

Each
\sf{lses}
comes with its own
Y
predicate and the role of Definition
2.7.8
and Definition
2.7.10
is to impose conditions that the
Y
predicate of a hod like
\sf{lses}
must have. One important point is that conditions like
\sf{R1}
and
\sf{R6}
depend on external factors. For example, in
\sf{R6}
we demand that
\iota_{\xi,1}={\rm ord}(\mathcal{O}^{{\mathcal{P}}}_{\delta_{\xi}+1,{\mathcal{P}}|\delta_{\xi}+1})
while there can be many ordinals
\alpha\in(\delta_{\xi},\iota_{\xi,1})
with the property that
{\mathcal{P}}|\alpha
is hod-like, yet none of them determine a layer. When designing
{\mathcal{P}}
via hod pair constructions (see Definition
4.3.3
), we will need to choose
\iota_{\xi,1}
, and its choice depends on the pointclass
\Gamma
that we attempt to generate via the hod pair construction. Intuitively,
\iota_{\xi,1}
is defined to be the ordinal height of the stack of all sound
\sf{ses}
over
{\mathcal{P}}|\delta_{\xi}+1
that are based on
{\mathcal{P}}|\delta_{\xi}
, have a projectum
\leq\delta_{\xi}
and have an iteration strategy in
\Gamma
.
\hfill\dashv

Remark 2.7.16
.

Continuing with the set up of Definition

\hfill\dashv

Next, we isolate the bottom part of

\sf{lses}

that is below the largest measurable limit of cutpoint Woodin cardinals.

Definition 2.7.18
(The bottom part of
\sf{lses}
).

Given a limit type hod-like
\sf{lses}

{\mathcal{P}}
we let

if

doesn’t have a top window and otherwise, letting

be the top window of
{\mathcal{P}}
, we let

{\mathcal{P}}^{b}={\mathcal{P}}|(\eta^{+})^{\mathcal{P}}

{\mathcal{P}}^{b}

bottom

{\mathcal{P}}
. It follows that

\sf{lses}
of limit type.

Similarly, if

is germane of
b
-type then

.

.

Remark 2.7.20
.

We are interested in germane
{\mathcal{M}}
that project precisely because we would like to apply stacks that are based on
{\sf{hl}}({\mathcal{M}})
to
{\mathcal{M}}
without changing the stack.

For example, assume
{\sf{hl}}({\mathcal{M}})=_{def}{\mathcal{P}}
and
{\mathcal{P}}
is a meek hod-like
\sf{lses}
of limit type. Suppose
{\mathcal{M}}
projects badly. If now
E\in\vec{E}^{{\mathcal{P}}|\delta^{\mathcal{P}}}
then
Ult({\mathcal{M}},E)
may have more layers than
Ult({\mathcal{P}},E)
, and
{\mathcal{P}}
’s strategy doesn’t act on these new layers. On the other hand if
{\mathcal{M}}
projects precisely then this is no longer the case as the functions used to compute
\pi^{\mathcal{M}}_{E}(\delta^{\mathcal{P}})
and
\pi^{\mathcal{P}}_{E}(\delta^{\mathcal{P}})
are the same, and they all are in
{\mathcal{P}}
.

We will use this sort of arguments later, when we need to show that if
{\mathcal{P}}
is full,
\Sigma
is its strategy,
{\mathcal{M}}
is germane such that
{\sf{hl}}({\mathcal{M}})={\mathcal{P}}
and
{\mathcal{M}}
is a
\Sigma
-mouse over
{\mathcal{P}}
then
{\mathcal{M}}
doesn’t project badly.

Notice that our comment above concerns only to germane
{\mathcal{M}}
which are not themselves hod-like. If
{\mathcal{M}}
is of
b
-type and projects across
{\rm ord}({\sf{hl}}({\mathcal{M}}))
but it does not project badly then
{\mathcal{M}}
itself is hod-like.

Summarizing, if
{\mathcal{M}}
projects precisely and
{\mathcal{T}}
is a stack on
{\sf{hl}}({\mathcal{M}})
then we define
\uparrow({\mathcal{T}},{\mathcal{M}})
just like we did in Definition
2.4.10
.
\hfill\dashv

2.8
The iteration embedding
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}

Recall our convention regarding stacks (see Remark
2.7.27
). In this section, we define the embedding
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}
via an inductive process. The reader may skip this section. The one important point that will come up later is the following. Suppose
\alpha\in R^{\mathcal{T}}
and
\beta<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
. Then if
\pi_{\alpha,\beta}^{{\mathcal{T}},b}
is defined then its domain is
({\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha}||(\omega\beta_{\alpha},m_{\alpha}))^{b}
which in general may not be the same as
{\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha}^{b}
.

Assume that
{\mathcal{P}}
is a limit type hod-like
\sf{lses}
which isn’t meek and suppose
{\mathcal{T}}
is an iteration tree on
{\mathcal{P}}
. Again, we will not be concerned with the particular indexing scheme that
{\mathcal{P}}
has. In some cases, regardless of whether
{\mathcal{T}}
has a last model or not, it is possible to extract an embedding out of the iteration embeddings given by
{\mathcal{T}}
that acts on
{\mathcal{P}}^{b}
. We describe this embedding below. First we define it by assuming that
{\mathcal{T}}
is a normal iteration tree and then extend the definition to stacks. Recall that our
\sf{lses}
are lsa-small (see Definition
2.7.4
).

Definition 2.8.1
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{P}}
is a non-meek hod-like
\sf{lses}
74
74

74

In particular,
{\mathcal{P}}\not={\mathcal{P}}^{b}
.
. Suppose

{\mathcal{T}}=(({\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha})_{\alpha<\eta},(E_{\alpha})_{\alpha<\eta-1},D,R,(\beta_{\alpha},m_{\alpha}),T)

is a normal iteration tree on
{\mathcal{P}}
. We define
(\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}:\alpha<\alpha^{\prime}<\eta\wedge(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime})\in T)
by induction maintaining that if
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}\not=\emptyset
then

(a) if
\alpha\not\in R
then
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}:{\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha}^{b}\rightarrow{\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha^{\prime}}^{b}
is an elementary embedding, and

(b) if
\alpha\in R
then
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}:({\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha}||(\omega\beta_{\alpha},m_{\alpha}))^{b}\rightarrow{\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha^{\prime}}^{b}
is an elementary embedding.

The successor case

Suppose
\beta+1<\eta
and we have defined
(\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}:\alpha<\alpha^{\prime}\leq\beta\wedge(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime})\in T)
. Let
\gamma^{\prime}={\mathcal{T}}(\beta+1)
. For
\gamma<\beta+1
such that
(\gamma,\beta+1)\in T
, we define
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta+1}
as follows.

1.

If
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{0,\gamma^{\prime}}=\emptyset
then set
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta+1}=\emptyset
.

In the next three clauses we assume that
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{0,\gamma^{\prime}}\not=\emptyset
and that
\gamma^{\prime}\not\in R
.

2.

Suppose
{\rm crit}(E_{\beta})>{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{b})
. Then set
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta+1}=\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}}
.

3.

Suppose
{\rm crit}(E_{\beta})\leq{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{b})
and
\beta+1\in D
. Then
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta+1}=\emptyset
.

4.

Suppose
{\rm crit}(E_{\beta})\leq{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{b})
and
\beta+1\not\in D
. Then
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta+1}=(\pi^{\mathcal{T}}_{\gamma^{\prime},\beta+1}\restriction{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{b})\circ\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}}
.

In the next three clauses we assume that
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{0,\gamma^{\prime}}\not=\emptyset
and that
\gamma^{\prime}\in R
.

5.

Suppose
{\rm crit}(E_{\beta})>{\rm ord}(({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}||(\omega\beta_{\gamma^{\prime}},m_{\gamma}^{\prime}))^{b})
. Then set
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta+1}=\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}}
.

6.

Suppose
{\rm crit}(E_{\beta})\leq{\rm ord}(({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}||(\omega\beta_{\gamma^{\prime}},m_{\gamma}^{\prime}))^{b})
and
\beta+1\in D
. Then
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta+1}=\emptyset
.

7.

Suppose
{\rm crit}(E_{\beta})\leq{\rm ord}(({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}||(\omega\beta_{\gamma^{\prime}},m_{\gamma}^{\prime}))^{b})
and
\beta+1\not\in D
. Then
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta+1}=(\pi^{\mathcal{T}}_{\gamma^{\prime},\beta+1}\restriction{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{b})\circ\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}}
.

The limit case

Suppose next that
\beta<\eta
is a limit ordinal and we have defined
(\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}:\alpha<\alpha^{\prime}<\beta\wedge(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime})\in T)
. Then we define
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta}
for
\gamma\in[0,\beta)_{\mathcal{T}}
according to the following cases:

1.

If
\gamma\in[0,\beta)_{\mathcal{T}}
is such that there is
\gamma^{\prime}\in[0,\beta)_{\mathcal{T}}
with the property that
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}}=\emptyset
then
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta}=\emptyset
.

2.

Suppose
\gamma\in[0,\beta)_{\mathcal{T}}
is such that for all
\gamma^{\prime}\in[0,\beta)_{\mathcal{T}}
,
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}}
is defined. Then letting
\nu+1\in b
be such that
T(\nu+1)=\gamma
,
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\gamma,\beta}=\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\nu+1,\beta}\circ\pi^{\mathcal{T}}_{\gamma,\nu+1}
where
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\nu+1,\beta}
is the direct limit embedding given by the directed system
({\mathcal{M}}_{\xi}^{b},\pi_{\xi,\xi^{\prime}}^{{\mathcal{T}},b}:\nu+1\leq\xi<\xi^{\prime}\wedge(\xi,\xi^{\prime})\in c^{2})
where
c=[0,\beta)_{\mathcal{T}}
.

The iteration embedding
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}

Continuing with the
{\mathcal{T}}
above, we let
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}
be defined according to the following clauses.

1.

Suppose
{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})=\gamma+1
. Then set
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}=\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{0,\gamma}
.

In all the clauses below we assume that
{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
is a limit ordinal.

2.

Suppose there is
\gamma<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
such that
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{0,\gamma}=\emptyset
and
{\mathcal{T}}_{\geq\gamma}
is a normal stack on
{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma}
. Then set
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}=\emptyset
.

In all the clauses below we assume that if
\gamma<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
is such that
{\mathcal{T}}_{\geq\gamma}
is a normal stack on
{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma}
then
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{0,\gamma}\not=\emptyset
.

3.

Suppose there is
\gamma<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
such that
{\mathcal{T}}_{\geq\gamma}
is a normal stack on
{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma}
based on
{\mathcal{M}}^{b}_{\gamma}
. Then set
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}=\emptyset
.

4.

Suppose there is
\gamma<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
such that
{\mathcal{T}}_{\geq\gamma}
is a normal stack on
{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma}
above
{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma}^{b})
. Then set
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}=\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{0,\gamma}
.

5.

Suppose there is a cofinal
c\subseteq{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
such that
\{\gamma<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}}):\exists\gamma^{\prime}\in c((\gamma,\gamma^{\prime})\in T)\}
is a well-founded branch of
{\mathcal{T}}
and for all
\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}
with
(\gamma,\gamma^{\prime})\in c^{2}
,
\pi_{0,\gamma}^{{\mathcal{T}},b}\not=\pi_{0,\gamma^{\prime}}^{{\mathcal{T}},b}
. Then set
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}=\pi^{{\mathcal{T}}}_{c}\restriction{\mathcal{P}}^{b}
.

Given
(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime})\in T
, we say
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}
is
defined
or
exists
if
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}\not=\emptyset
. Similarly we say
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}
is
defined
or
exists
if
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}\not=\emptyset
.
\hfill\dashv

Remark 2.8.2
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{P}}
is a non-meek hod-like
\sf{lses}
and
{\mathcal{T}}
is a stack on
{\mathcal{P}}
. For all
\alpha<\alpha^{\prime}
such that
(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime})\in T
, if
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}
exists then it is essentially the iteration embedding. However, given how
\pi_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{T}}
is defined, it is possible that
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}
exists yet
\pi_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{T}}
is undefined.

In general, we have that
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}
is defined if and only if for all
\gamma
such that
\gamma+1\in[\alpha,\alpha^{\prime})_{\mathcal{T}}\cap D^{\mathcal{T}}
,
{\rm crit}(E_{\gamma})>{\rm ord}({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma}^{b})
.
\hfill\dashv

Notice that in Definition
2.8.1
we are not assuming that the stack has a last model. The fragment of the eventual iteration embedding
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}}}
restricted to
{\mathcal{P}}^{b}
can be seen without actually having the last branch.

2.9
Canonical singularizing sequence

The following notion will be used throughout this paper.

Definition 2.9.1
(Canonical singularizing sequences).

Suppose
{\mathcal{P}}
is a germane
\sf{lses}
of
b
-type that projects precisely and
{\mathcal{T}}
is an almost non-dropping stack on
{\mathcal{P}}
. Let
{\mathcal{Q}}=\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}({\mathcal{P}}^{b})
. Then
{\mathcal{Q}}
is a hod-like
\sf{lses}
. If
w=(\eta,\delta)
is a window of
{\mathcal{Q}}
then we let

s({\mathcal{T}},w)=\{\alpha:\exists a\in\eta^{<\omega}\exists f\in{\mathcal{P}}^{b}(\alpha=\pi^{{\mathcal{T}},b}(f)(a))\}\cap\delta

\hfill\dashv

The following is an easy lemma, which is a consequence of our assumption that all hod-like
{\sf{lses}}
are lsa small. It traces back to the fact that if
{\mathcal{P}}
is a hod-like
{\sf{lses}}
and
E\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{P}}
is an extender such that
{\rm crit}(E)=\delta^{\mathcal{Q}}
for some layer
{\mathcal{Q}}
of
{\mathcal{P}}
and
\nu\in[{\rm crit}(E),{\rm ind}^{\mathcal{P}}(E)]
then
Ult({\mathcal{P}},E)\vDash``\nu
is not a Woodin cardinal”.

u\in[{\rm ind}_{\beta}]^{<\omega}
there is
u^{\prime}\in[{\rm ind}_{\beta}]^{<\omega}
such that if
\pi_{\gamma,\alpha}(f)(u)
is defined then
\pi_{\gamma,\alpha}(f)(u)=\pi_{0,\alpha}(h)(u^{\prime})
. It then follows from (4) that
\sup(s({\mathcal{T}},w))=\delta
.

2.10
The un-dropping game

Recall our convention regarding proper stacks (see Remark
2.7.27
).
Before we proceed, we explain the meaning of the un-dropping game. Suppose we are comparing the strategies of two lsa type hod-like
\sf{lses}

{\mathcal{P}}
and
{\mathcal{Q}}
. Let
\Sigma
be the strategy of
{\mathcal{P}}
and
\Lambda
be the strategy of
{\mathcal{Q}}
. Let us assume that the pointclasses generated by
({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
and
({\mathcal{Q}},\Lambda)
are the same. We are then searching for
{\mathcal{R}}
which is an iterate of
{\mathcal{P}}
and
{\mathcal{Q}}
and
\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}}=\Lambda_{\mathcal{R}}
. In this comparison we might be forced to consider iteration trees
{\mathcal{T}}
and
{\mathcal{U}}
with last models
{\mathcal{M}}
and
{\mathcal{N}}
such that
\pi^{\mathcal{T}}
and
\pi^{\mathcal{U}}
don’t exist and for some
{\mathcal{K}}\trianglelefteq_{hod}{\mathcal{M}}
and
{\mathcal{K}}\trianglelefteq_{hod}{\mathcal{N}}
,
\Sigma_{{\mathcal{K}}}\not=\Lambda_{{\mathcal{K}}}
. We can continue the comparison by comparing
({\mathcal{M}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}})
and
({\mathcal{N}},\Lambda_{\mathcal{N}})
and producing
({\mathcal{S}},\Phi)
which is a common tail of
({\mathcal{M}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}})
and
({\mathcal{N}},\Lambda_{\mathcal{N}})
. However,
({\mathcal{S}},\Phi)
cannot be thought of as a last model of a successful comparison of
({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
and
({\mathcal{Q}},\Lambda)
simply because
\pi^{\mathcal{T}}
and
\pi^{\mathcal{U}}
do not exist. What we need to do is to compare
({\mathcal{M}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}})
and
({\mathcal{N}},\Lambda_{\mathcal{N}})
and then somehow get back to
{\mathcal{P}}
and
{\mathcal{Q}}
. This is what the un-dropping game achieves.

{\mathcal{P}}={\mathcal{M}}_{0}
\dots
{\mathcal{R}}_{i}
\triangledown
{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}
{\mathcal{R}}_{i+1}
\triangledown
{\mathcal{Q}}_{i+1}
\dots
{\mathcal{R}}_{k}
\triangledown
{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}
{\mathcal{T}}_{i}
{\mathcal{T}}_{i+1}
{\mathcal{T}}_{k}

A stack with neat drops.

Terminology 2.10.4

Definition 2.10.6
(The un-dropping iteration game).

Suppose
{\mathcal{P}}
is a germane,
b
-type
\sf{lses}
that projects precisely. The un-dropping iteration game on
{\mathcal{P}}
,

1.

In
\mathcal{G}^{u}({\mathcal{P}},\kappa,\lambda,\alpha)
, player I and II collaborate to produce a sequence

p=({\mathcal{M}}_{\beta},{\mathcal{T}}_{\beta},{\mathcal{Q}}_{\beta},E_{\beta}:\beta<\gamma)

such that

(a)

\gamma\leq\kappa
,

(b)

{\mathcal{M}}_{0}={\mathcal{P}}
,

(c)

for all
\beta<\gamma
,
{\mathcal{T}}_{\beta}
is a stack on
{\mathcal{M}}_{\beta}
(and is produced via the rules of
\mathcal{G}({\mathcal{M}}_{\beta},\lambda,\alpha)
88
88

88

This is the game defined in
[
60
, Chapter 4]
.
),

(d)

for each
\beta
such that
\beta+1<\gamma

\pi^{p}_{0,\beta}:{\mathcal{M}}_{0}\rightarrow{\mathcal{M}}_{\beta}
is defined,

(e)

for each
\beta
such that
\beta+1<\gamma
, either

i.

E_{\beta}
is the
{\mathcal{Q}}_{\beta}
- un-dropping extender of
{\mathcal{T}}_{\beta}
and
{\mathcal{M}}_{\beta+1}=Ult({\mathcal{M}}_{\beta},E_{\beta})
,

or

,
\pi^{{\mathcal{T}}_{\beta}}
exists and
{\mathcal{M}}_{\beta+1}
is the last model of
{\mathcal{T}}_{\beta}
,

(f)

for a limit ordinal
\beta<\gamma

(g)

is ill-founded.

on

and

. Since

there is no ambiguity in omitting
{\mathcal{Q}}_{\beta}
s.

The next definition introduces
self-cohering
iteration strategies. The idea is as follows. Suppose
{\mathcal{P}}
is a non-meek hod-like
{\sf{lses}}

{\mathcal{R}}
be the last model of
{\mathcal{T}}_{0}
. Then
{\mathcal{R}}^{b}\trianglelefteq{\mathcal{M}}_{1}^{b}
. But it is not clear that
\Sigma_{{\mathcal{R}}^{b},{\mathcal{T}}_{0}}=\Sigma_{{\mathcal{R}}^{b},{\mathcal{T}}_{0}^{\frown}\{F_{0}\}}
. Self-cohering strategies have this property. We will use this property in our diamond comparison argument (see Definition
4.14
).

Definition 2.10.10
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{T}}
is a stack and
{\mathcal{R}}={\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha}^{\mathcal{T}}
for some
\alpha<{\rm lh}({\mathcal{T}})
. We then say that

Chapter 3
Short tree strategy mice

The main purpose of this chapter is to isolate the definition of short tree strategy mice. As was mentioned many times before, the main problem with defining this concept is the fact that it is possible that maximal iteration trees (which should not have branches indexed in the strategy predicate) may
core down
to short iteration trees (which must have branches indexed in the strategy predicate), thus causing indexing issues. To solve this issue we will design an authentication procedure which will carefully choose iteration trees and index their branches. Thus, if some iteration tree doesn’t have a branch indexed in the strategy predicate then it is because the authentication procedure hasn’t yet found an authenticated branch, and therefore, such iteration trees cannot core down to an iteration tree whose branch is authenticated.

The following is a rough roadmap of the chapter. Section
3.1
introduces the short tree component of an iteration strategy, while Section
3.2
introduces the short tree strategy as an abstract object. This is an important step as the strategy predicate of a short tree strategy mouse codes a short tree strategy in the sense of Definition
3.2.4
. The next important step is the isolation of two different kinds of iterations, those that are universally short (see Definition
3.3.2
), i.e. short with respect to any strategy, and those that are ambiguous. As there is no ambiguity involved in determining whether a universally short iteration trees are short or not and moreover, since universal shortness is preserved under Mostowski collapses, we will simply add the branches of such iterations to the strategy predicate without authenticating them first. The branches of ambiguous iterations will be authenticated before being added to the strategy predicate.

A key tool in the authentication procedure is the fully backgrounded constructions that produce iterates of hod like
{\sf{lses}}
(see Definition
3.5.1
). Such constructions are used to find a branch of an iteration tree with the property that the branch model itself iterates to the same construction. Definition
3.6.4
and Definition
3.8.7
introduce the particular ways branches will be indexed. Our authentication procedure appears as Definition
3.7.3
, and Definition
3.8.9
defines indexing scheme. Then Definition
3.8.17
introduces the short tree strategy mice and Remark
3.8.20
explains exactly how branches get indexed. Definition
3.10.2
finally introduces the concept of a hod premouse.

Remark 3.0.1
.

All the notions introduced in this chapter can be routinely carried over to germane
\sf{lses}
that project precisely. Thus, when discussing germane
\sf{lses}
, we will freely use the language developed in the sections of this chapter.
\hfill\dashv

Remark 3.2.6
.

In many situations, it is expected that finding
(\kappa,\lambda)
-st-strategies must be easy. For example, whenever
{\mathcal{T}}
is normal iteration tree of length
\omega
such that
\mathcal{J}_{\omega}({\rm m}^{+}({\mathcal{T}}))\vDash``\delta({\mathcal{T}})
is a Woodin”, we can set
\Lambda({\mathcal{T}})={\rm m}^{+}({\mathcal{T}})
. Thus, instead of working hard to define the correct branch, we declare success by setting
\Lambda({\mathcal{T}})={\rm m}^{+}({\mathcal{T}})
. However, we will be interested in st-strategies that have certain fullness preservation properties. For instance, suppose
{\mathcal{M}}
is just a suitable mouse in the sense of
L(\mathbb{R})
. If we now demand that
\Lambda
must have the property that whenever
{\mathcal{T}}\in{\rm dom}(\Lambda)
is such that
{\mathcal{Q}}({\mathcal{T}})
exists then
\Lambda({\mathcal{T}})
must be a branch
b
with the property that
{\mathcal{Q}}(b,{\mathcal{T}})={\mathcal{Q}}({\mathcal{T}})
then
\Lambda
would be a rather complex object. We will have that
\Lambda({\mathcal{T}})
is a model only in the case when
{\mathcal{T}}
is a maximal iteration tree. In this case,
\Lambda
is in fact a “short tree iterability strategy” in the sense of
L(\mathbb{R})
. Such strategies are difficult to construct, and in our current situation, we will be interested in a notion of fullness preservation with respect to a much more complicated pointclass than
(\Sigma^{2}_{1})^{L(\mathbb{R})}
.
\hfill\dashv

3.3
Hull and branch condensation for short tree strategy

The goal of this section is to introduce
hull condensation
for st-strategies. Hull condensation for iteration strategies was introduced in Definition 1.31 of
[
30
]
. It is an important property that is used to show that when doing hod pair constructions no discrepancies arise due to the coring down process. Thus if
{\mathcal{T}}
is according to a strategy with hull condensation and
{\mathcal{U}}
is a
hull
of
{\mathcal{T}}
(cf. Definition
3.3.4
) then it is according to the strategy.

The difference between strategies and st-strategies is that st-strategies have a model component, and this difference causes some complications when trying to outright generalize hull condensation: such a direct generalization leads to a very strong property. Our definition is based on our indexing scheme Definition
3.6.4
. In short tree strategy mice, we only index branches of a certain kinds of iterations, and we need to apply hull condensation to these types of iterations. We start by introducing these iterations.

First we define the
universally short normal trees
which are essentially those normal iteration trees that are short with respect to any iteration strategy.

3.4

Suppose

The above scenario is the main difficulty with defining short tree strategy mice. We have to find a particular indexing of short tree strategies, or rather carefully skip over “bad trees”, in a way that when

above is “cored down” to

above then our indexing is still preserved. In particular, the branch of
{\mathcal{T}}

{\mathcal{T}}

-structure is

. Before we define short tree hybrids, however, we have to make a few definitions that will be useful to us in the future.

In this manuscript, our goal is to deal with novel issues arising from the theory of short tree strategy mice, such as developing an indexing scheme for short tree strategies, proving a comparison theorem for lsa small hod pairs and obtain core model induction applications at the level of
\sf{LSA}

Remark 3.5.2
.

Notice that the constructions introduced in Definition
3.5.1
can be carried out even when
\Sigma
is a partial strategy. Thus, for example, we may say that
``(({\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma},{\mathcal{N}}_{\gamma}:\gamma\leq\eta),(F_{\gamma}:\gamma<\eta),({\mathcal{T}}_{\gamma}:\gamma\leq\eta))

is the output of the
({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
-coherent fully backgrounded construction of
N"
the meaning of which should be self-evident with one wrinkle. It may be that for some
\gamma\leq\eta
,
\Sigma({\mathcal{T}}_{\gamma})
is undefined. In this case, we have that
\gamma=\eta
and we stop the construction.

If the background universe has a distinguished extender sequence then we tacitly assume that the extenders appearing in the
({\mathcal{P}},\Sigma)
-coherent fully background construction come from this distinguished extender sequence.

3.6
A short tree strategy indexing scheme

Our goal here is to introduce the notion of a
short tree strategy premouse
(
sts premouse
). As we mentioned in the previous section, the difficulty with doing this lies in the fact that maximal trees might “core down” to short trees and thus, creating indexing issues. The idea behind the solution presented here is to add a branch for a tree as soon as we see a certificate of shortness, which in our case will be a
{\mathcal{Q}}
-structure. As the
{\mathcal{Q}}
-structures that we will be looking for are themselves sts premice, this inevitably leads to an induction.

Technically speaking
{\mathcal{M}}
in Definition
3.6.2
should not be
{\sf{ses}}
(see Definition
2.5.2
) as
f^{\mathcal{N}}
doesn’t quite code an iteration strategy. Its domain consists of indexable stacks (see Definition
3.3.3
). But recall the abuse of terminology proposed after Definition
2.5.1
. Also, recall the definition of
{\rm m}^{+}({\mathcal{T}})={\rm m}({\mathcal{T}})^{\#}
(see Definition
3.1.4
).

The language of unindexed
\sf{ses}
33
33

33

See Definition
2.5.3
.
includes constant symbols for
\vec{E}
,
f
,
X
and
{\mathcal{P}}
. We denote these symbols by
\dot{E}
,
\dot{f}
,
\dot{X}
and
\dot{{\mathcal{P}}}
. Also, we let
\dot{<}
be the symbol denoting the constructibility order and
\dot{\Sigma}
be the partial strategy coded by
\dot{f}
.
\dot{<}
and
\dot{\Sigma}
are not symbols in the language but they can be easily defined from the other symbols.

Definition 3.6.1
(
\phi^{*}
-formula).

We let
\phi^{*}(x)
be the conjunction of the following statements in the language of
\sf{ses}
.

1.

x
is a sequential structure of the form

3.8

46

46

The meaning of this is the following. For each

be
\beta
