.

The following statements can be easily verified using the definitions and our assumption.

Proposition 11.3.1
.

For a club of
\tau\in{\mathcal{S}}
:

1.

o({\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau})>\tau
,

2.

\gamma_{\tau}\geq\tau
.

Proof.

By the construction of
{\mathcal{S}}
, for any
\tau\in{\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{P}}|\tau
is passive and is a
\sf{ZFC}^{-}
-model, and therefore
\rho_{\omega}^{{\mathcal{P}}|\tau}=\tau
. This means
o({\mathcal{P}}|\tau)<o({\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau})
. This proves (1).

For (2), suppose not. Then there is a stationary set of
\tau\in{\mathcal{S}}
such that
\gamma_{\tau}<\tau
. By pressing down, there is a stationary set
T\subset{\mathcal{S}}
and a
\gamma<\kappa^{+}
such that for all
\tau\in T
,

\gamma_{\tau}=\gamma<\tau.

But then since the sequence
(\gamma_{\tau}:\tau\in{\mathcal{S}})
is monotonically non-decreasing, this means that

\textrm{sup}_{\tau\in{\mathcal{S}}}(\gamma_{\tau})=\gamma<\kappa.

This contradicts our assumption.

Extenders
E
with cr
(E)=\mu
play a special role in this construction. Note that
\mu
is a strong cutpoint of
{\mathcal{P}}^{b}
, that is, there are no partial extenders with critical point
\mu
on the sequence of
{\mathcal{P}}
. This is the main difference between our situation and the
L[E]
-situation. It is this situation that forces us to consider collapsing structures that are not initial segments of our hod mouse
{\mathcal{P}}
.

Some discussions regarding protomice and divisors are in order. Following
[
39
]
, for a hod premouse
{\mathcal{N}}
such that
\omega\rho^{n+1}_{\mathcal{N}}\leq\kappa<\omega\rho^{n}_{\mathcal{N}}
, we say that
(\nu,q)
is a
divisor
of
{\mathcal{N}}
if and only if there is an ordinal
\lambda=\lambda_{\mathcal{N}}(\nu,q)
such that letting
p_{\mathcal{N}}
be the (
n+1
)-st standard parameter of
{\mathcal{N}}
, setting
r=p_{\mathcal{N}}-q
, the following hold:

(a)

\nu\leq\kappa<\lambda<\omega\rho^{n}_{\mathcal{N}}
;

(b)

q=p_{\mathcal{N}}\cap\lambda
;

(c)

\tilde{h}^{n+1}_{\mathcal{N}}(\nu\cup\{r\})\cap\omega\rho^{n}_{\mathcal{N}}
is cofinal in
\omega\rho^{n}_{\mathcal{N}}
;

(d)

\lambda=\rm{min}(\rm{OR}
\cap\tilde{h}^{n+1}_{\mathcal{N}}(\nu\cup\{r\})-\nu)
.

As in
[
39
]
, both
\nu
and
\lambda
are (inaccessible) cardinals in
{\mathcal{N}}
. Let
{\mathcal{N}}^{*}(\nu,q)
be the transitive collapse of
\tilde{h}^{n+1}_{\mathcal{N}}(\nu\cup\{r\})
.

The notion of strong divisors in
[
39
]
generalize in an obvious way to our context. We recall it now. A divisor
(\nu,q)
of
{\mathcal{N}}
is
strong
if and only if for every
\xi<\nu
and every
x
of the form
\tilde{h}^{n+1}_{\mathcal{N}}(\xi,p_{\mathcal{N}})
we have
x\cap\nu\in{\mathcal{N}}^{*}(\nu,q)
. If
{\mathcal{N}}
is pluripotent, we define the notion of strong divisor in the same way, but with
h^{*}_{\mathcal{N}}
(the
\Sigma_{1}
-Skolem function of
{\mathcal{N}}
computed in the language of coherent structures) and
d_{\mathcal{N}}
(the Dodd-parameter of
{\mathcal{N}}
) in place of
\tilde{h}^{n+1}_{\mathcal{N}}
and
p_{\mathcal{N}}
, respectively. It turns out, see
[
39
, Section 2]
, that the notion of divisor/strong divisor does not depend on which language one uses to compute it.

As in
[
39
]
, if
{\mathcal{N}}
has strong divisors,
the canonical strong divisor

(\mu_{\mathcal{N}},q_{\mathcal{N}})
of
{\mathcal{N}}
is chosen as follows:
q_{\mathcal{N}}
is the shortest initial segment of
p_{\mathcal{N}}
such that for some
\nu^{*}
,
(\nu^{*},q_{\mathcal{N}})
is a strong divisor of
{\mathcal{N}}
and
\mu_{\mathcal{N}}
is the largest
\nu^{*}
such that
(\nu^{*},q_{\mathcal{N}})
is a strong divisor of
{\mathcal{N}}
. Now we define our collapsing structure
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
for
\tau\in{\mathcal{S}}
.

Definition 11.3.2
.

Fix
\tau\in{\mathcal{S}}
. Suppose there is a pointclass
\Omega\subsetneq\Gamma
such that there is a hod pair
({\mathcal{R}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}})
such that

(i)

{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau}|\gamma_{\tau}\lhd{\mathcal{R}}
,

(ii)

\rho^{\omega}_{\mathcal{R}}=\kappa
,

(iii)

\gamma_{\tau}
is a cutpoint of
{\mathcal{R}}
and
\Sigma_{{\mathcal{R}}|{\gamma_{\tau}}}=\Sigma_{{\mathcal{P}}|{\gamma_{\tau}}}
,

(iv)

{\mathcal{R}}
is
\gamma_{\tau}
-sound,

(v)

the order type of
{\mathcal{R}}
’s layer Woodin cardinals above
\gamma_{\tau}
is a limit ordinal,

(vi)

{\mathcal{R}}
has a strong divisor of the form
(\mu,q)
where
p_{\mathcal{R}}=q\cup r
for
r
above the supremum
\lambda
of the layer Woodin cardinals of
{\mathcal{R}}
and max
(q)
is below
(\gamma_{\tau}^{+})^{\mathcal{R}}
and
(\gamma_{\tau}^{+})^{\mathcal{R}}<\lambda
,

(vii)

\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}}
has branch condensation, is
\Omega
-fullness preserving, and
({\mathcal{R}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}})
generates
\Omega
; that is
\Gamma({\mathcal{R}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}})=\Omega
.

We call
({\mathcal{R}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}})
with the above properties the pointclass generator of
\Omega
. Let
\Gamma_{\tau}
be the Wadge-minimal such pointclass and
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
be the pointclass generator of
\Gamma_{\tau}
,
(\mu_{\tau},q_{\tau},\lambda_{\tau})
be the
(\mu,q,\lambda)
associated with
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
as above (note that
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
must be distinct from
{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau}
in this case). If
(\Gamma_{\tau},{\mathcal{R}},\mu,q,\lambda)
doesn’t exist, we let
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}={\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau}
.
\hfill\dashv

The properties of pointclass generators seem technical; these properties are abstracted from various situations in interpolation arguments. It seems hard to do with much less. Here is a very rough explanation for why we would consider such objects before going into details: suppose
(\Gamma_{\tau},{\mathcal{R}},\mu,q,\lambda)
exists, then letting
\pi:{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau}(\mu,q)\rightarrow{\mathcal{R}}
be the uncollapse map and
F
be the
(\mu,\gamma_{\tau})
-extender derived from
\pi
. Letting
{\mathcal{R}}^{*}\lhd{\mathcal{P}}|\mu^{+}
be the largest such that
\rho_{\omega}^{\mathcal{S}}=\mu
and
{\wp}(\mu)\cap{\mathcal{R}}^{*}={\wp}(\mu)\cap{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau}(\mu,q)
., then we can show that
{\mathcal{R}}=\textrm{Ult}({\mathcal{R}}^{*},F)
. Since
{\wp}(\mu)\cap{\mathcal{R}}^{*}\subsetneq{\wp}(\mu)\cap{\mathcal{P}}
,
{\mathcal{R}}
belongs to
\Gamma
and will generate a pointclass (
\Gamma_{\tau}
) strictly smaller than
\Gamma
. It turns out that there is a unique such
({\mathcal{R}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}})
that generates
\Gamma_{\tau}
. This canonicity is important in the
\square
-construction.

The following proposition justifies the uniqueness of pointclass generators.

Proposition 11.3.3
.

Let
{\mathcal{P}},\tau,\Omega
be as in Definition
11.3.2
. Let
({\mathcal{R}}_{0},\Sigma_{0})
and
({\mathcal{R}}_{1},\Sigma_{1})
be pointclass generators of
\Omega
with the properties described in
11.3.2
. Then
({\mathcal{R}}_{0},\Sigma_{0})=({\mathcal{R}}_{1},\Sigma_{1})
.

Proof.

We compare the pair
({\mathcal{R}}_{0},\Sigma_{0})
against
({\mathcal{R}}_{1},\Sigma_{1})
, lining up the models and the strategies (as done in Section
4.13
). The comparison is possible by the assumption, namely
\Gamma({\mathcal{R}}_{0},\Sigma_{0})=\Gamma({\mathcal{R}}_{1},\Sigma_{1})=\Omega
, and is above
\gamma_{\tau}
(this is because
\gamma_{\tau}
is a cutpoint, in fact a strong cutpoint, of both models and
{\mathcal{R}}_{0}|\gamma_{\tau}={\mathcal{R}}_{1}|\gamma_{\tau}
). The end model is, say,
{\mathcal{S}}
and the tail strategies of
\Sigma_{0}
and
\Sigma_{1}
on
{\mathcal{S}}
are the same. The usual proof using the fact that
{\mathcal{R}}_{0}
and
{\mathcal{R}}_{1}
are
\gamma_{\tau}
-sound and the comparison is above
\gamma_{\tau}
shows that
{\mathcal{S}}={\mathcal{R}}_{0}={\mathcal{R}}_{1}
(the comparison is trivial) and
\Sigma_{0}=\Sigma_{1}
. The equality of models (i.e.
{\mathcal{R}}_{0}={\mathcal{R}}_{1}
) follows from the fact that
({\mathcal{R}}_{0},\Sigma_{0})
and
({\mathcal{R}}_{1},\Sigma_{1})
generate the same pointclass. Otherwise, say
{\mathcal{R}}_{0}={\mathcal{R}}_{1}(\alpha)\lhd{\mathcal{R}}_{1}
for some
\alpha
and
\Sigma_{0}=(\Sigma_{1})_{{\mathcal{R}}_{0}}

Proposition 11.3.6

Suppose

Proof.

Fix

Now let

-sequence such that cr

to go through in this situation. The traditional approach to indexing branches does not seem to imply that

is a hod premouse.

It remains to see that
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}
is indeed

. We apply Theorem

. (a) cannot hold since the map

is a

is sound. So (b) holds; in fact,

Lemma 11.3.14
.

D
is a closed subset of
\tau
.

Proof.

Let
\tilde{\tau}
be a limit point of
D
. We show that
\tilde{\tau}\in D
. Form the direct limit
\langle\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}},\sigma_{\bar{\tau}\tilde{\tau}}\ |\ \bar{\tau}\in D\cap\tilde{\tau}\rangle
of the system
\langle{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\bar{\tau}},\sigma_{\tau^{*}\bar{\tau}}\ |\ \tau^{*}\leq\bar{\tau}\wedge\tau^{*},\bar{\tau}\in D\cap\tilde{\tau}\rangle
. The direct limit is well-founded and there is a
\Sigma_{0}
embedding
\sigma:\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
(defined by
\sigma(\sigma_{\bar{\tau}\tilde{\tau}}(x))=\sigma_{\bar{\tau},\tau}(x)
). It is easy to check that:

(a)

\sigma\circ\sigma_{\bar{\tau}\tilde{\tau}}=\sigma_{\bar{\tau}\tau}
.

(b)

\tilde{\tau}=\sigma_{\bar{\tau}\tilde{\tau}}(\bar{\tau})
,
\sigma_{\tilde{\tau}\tau}(\tilde{\tau})=\tau
, and
\tilde{\tau}=\rm{cr}(\sigma)
.

(c)

\sigma
is
\Sigma_{0}^{(n)}
preserving where
n=n_{\tau}
(with respect to the language of coherent structures).

We need to see that
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}={\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tilde{\tau}}
. First, we show that
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}
is a hod premouse of the same type as
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
. Note that
\Pi_{2}
-properties which hold on a tail end are upward preserved under direct limit maps (cf.
[
39
, pg 8-9]
). Furthermore,
{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\bar{\tau}}
is of the same type as
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
for each
\bar{\tau}\in D\cap\tau
. So
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}
is of the same type as
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
(as either a passive hod premouse, or a
B
-active hod premouse, or an
E
-active hod premouse with cr
(E^{\rm{top}}_{\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}})>\mu
, in which case
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}
is of type
A
, or else an
E
-active hod premouse with cr
(E^{\rm{top}}_{\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}})=\mu
, in which case
\omega\rho^{1}_{\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}}>\kappa
; these statements can be expressed in a
\Pi_{2}
-fashion).

Recall that for
\bar{\tau}\in D
, we use
\tilde{h}_{\bar{\tau}}
to denote
\tilde{h}^{(n_{\bar{\tau}}+1)}_{{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\bar{\tau}}}
, the
\Sigma_{1}^{(n_{\bar{\tau}})}
-Skolem function of
{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\bar{\tau}}
. Here note that
n_{\bar{\tau}}=n_{\tau}=n
. Let
\tilde{p}=\sigma_{\bar{\tau}\tilde{\tau}}(p^{*}_{\bar{\tau}})
for
\bar{\tau}\in D\cap\tilde{\tau}
. Given any
x\in\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}
, there is
\bar{\tau}\in D\cap\tilde{\tau}
and
\bar{x}\in{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\bar{\tau}}
such that
x=\sigma_{\bar{\tau}\tau}(\bar{x})
. There is
\xi<\kappa
such that
\bar{x}=\tilde{h}_{\bar{\tau}}(\xi,p_{\bar{\tau}})
. This
\Sigma^{(n)}_{1}
-statement is preserved by
\sigma_{\bar{\tau}\tilde{\tau}}
, so

. So
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}=\tilde{h}^{n+1}_{\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}}(\kappa\cup\{\tilde{p}\})
.

This gives
\omega\rho^{n+1}_{\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}}=\omega\rho^{\omega}_{\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}}\leq\kappa
. But
\kappa
is a cardinal in
{\mathcal{P}}
, so we indeed have equality. For each
\alpha\in p_{\tau}
, there is a generalized witness for
\alpha
with respect to
({\mathcal{N}}_{\tau},p_{\tau})
in range of
\sigma
. This is because rng
(\sigma)
contains rng
(\sigma_{\bar{\tau},\tau})
for any
\bar{\tau}\in D\cap\tilde{\tau}
and rng
(\sigma_{\bar{\tau},\tau})
contains such a witness. This takes care of (c) in the definition of
D
. This easily implies that
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}
is sound and
\tilde{p}
is the standard paramter of
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}
. We can now apply Theorem
11.1.5
as in the proof of Lemma
11.3.13
to conclude that
\tilde{{\mathcal{N}}}={\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tilde{\tau}}
.

Lemma 11.3.19
.

B^{1}_{\tau}-\bar{\tau}=D-\bar{\tau}
.

Proof.

We need to prove that there is
\bar{\tau}<\tau
such that for every
\tau^{\prime}\in D-\bar{\tau}
,
(\mu_{\tau},q^{*}_{\bar{\tau}})=(\mu_{\tau^{\prime}},q_{\tau^{\prime}})
. Assume for contradiction that there is a sequence
\langle\tau_{i}\ |\ i<\delta\rangle
that is increasing, cofinal in
\tau
such that
(\mu_{\tau_{i}},q_{\tau_{i}})\neq(\mu_{\tau},q^{*}_{\tau_{i}})
. We may assume without loss of generality that the sequence
\langle\mu_{\tau_{i}}\ |\ i<\delta\rangle
is monotonic and all
q_{\tau_{i}}
’s have the same length, say
m
.

If
\mu_{\tau}=\mu
, then we claim that for each
i<\delta
,
(\mu_{\tau_{i}},q_{\tau_{i}})=(\mu_{\tau},q^{*}_{\tau_{i}})
. This follows from the proof of Lemma
11.3.15
, where we prove that in this case, for each
i<\delta
,
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau_{i}}\neq{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau_{i}}
and
\mu_{\tau_{i}}=\mu=\mu_{\tau}
and
q_{\tau_{i}}=q^{*}_{\tau_{i}}
. This contradicts the assumption that
(\mu_{\tau_{i}},q_{\tau_{i}})\neq(\mu_{\tau},q^{*}_{\tau_{i}})
. So we must have that
\mu_{\tau}>\mu
, so
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}={\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau}
. This implies that for each
i<\delta
,
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau_{i}}={\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau_{i}}
(again, by remarks in Section
11.3.1
and the argument in Lemma
11.3.15
). So it must be the case then that
\mu_{\tau_{i}}>\mu
(note that since
{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau_{i}}={\mathcal{N}}_{\tau_{i}}
,
{\mathcal{N}}^{*}_{\tau_{i}}
cannot have strong divisors of the form
(\mu,q)
for some
q
) and so
(\mu_{\tau_{i}},q_{\tau_{i}})
, by definition, is the canonical strong divisor of
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau_{i}}
.

By the definition of
(\mu_{\tau_{i}},q_{\tau_{i}})
, each
q_{\tau_{i}}
is a bottom part of
q^{*}_{\tau_{i}}
, say
q^{*}_{\tau_{i}}=q_{\tau_{i}}\cup s_{\tau_{i}}
(
s_{\tau_{i}}
may be empty). Recall we have shown
\mu_{\tau},\mu_{\tau_{i}}>\mu
(so we can freely quote results of
[
39
, Section 2.4 and Lemma 3.12]
in the arguments that follow). Now we observe that
\mu_{\tau_{i}}>\mu_{\tau}
for all
i<\delta
. This is because the argument in
[
39
, Lemma 3.12]
shows: if
q_{\tau_{i}}=q^{*}_{\tau_{i}}
, then
\mu_{\tau_{i}}
must be
>\mu_{\tau}
by maximality of
\mu_{\tau_{i}}
for
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau_{i}}
and the assumption that
(\mu_{\tau},q^{*}_{\tau_{i}})\neq(\mu_{\tau_{i}},q_{\tau_{i}})
; otherwise,
q_{\tau_{i}}
is a strict bottom segment of
q^{*}_{\tau_{i}}
, and hence
[
39
, Lemma 2.26]
shows that no
\nu\leq\mu_{\tau}
is such that
(\nu,q_{\tau_{i}})
is a strong divisor of
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau_{i}}
.

Set for some (equivalently for all sufficiently large)
i<\delta
,
q=\sigma_{\tau_{i}\tau}(q_{\tau_{i}})
,
s=\sigma_{\tau_{i}\tau}(s_{\tau_{i}})
,
r=r_{\tau}
,
\nu=\rm{sup}
{}_{i<\delta}\mu_{\tau_{i}}
. Now
(\nu,q)
is a divisor of
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
(see
[
39
, Lemma 3.12]
). Since
\nu>\mu_{\tau}>\mu
,
(\nu,q)
cannot be a strong divisor of
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}
. Then a calculation as in
[
39
, Lemma 3.12]
shows that for some
i<\delta
,
(\mu_{\tau_{i}},q_{\tau_{i}})
is not a strong divisor of
{\mathcal{N}}_{\tau_{i}}
. Contradiction.

Lemmata

11.3.18

together complete the proof of Lemma

in the case

Chapter 12
\sf{LSA}
from
\sf{PFA}

For a cardinal
\kappa
, let
{\wp}_{0}(\kappa)=\kappa
;
{\wp}_{n+1}(\kappa)=2^{{\wp}_{n}(\kappa)}
for all

.

Definition 12.0.1
.

A sequence
\langle\vec{C}_{\alpha}\ |\ \alpha\in\lambda\rangle
is a
\square(\kappa,\lambda)
sequence if it satisfies the following properties.

(i)

0<|\vec{C}_{\alpha}|<\kappa
for all limit
\alpha\in\lambda
.

(ii)

C\subseteq\alpha
is club in
\alpha
for all limit
\alpha\in\lambda
and
C\in\vec{C}_{\alpha}
.

(iii)

C\cap\beta\in\vec{C}_{\beta}
for all limit
\alpha\in\lambda
,
C\in\vec{C}_{\alpha}
and
\beta\in\rm{Lim}
(C)
.

(iv)

There is no club
D\subseteq\lambda
such that
D\cap\alpha\in\vec{C}_{\alpha}
for all
\alpha\in\rm{Lim}
(D)
.

We say that
\square(\kappa,\lambda)
holds if a
\square(\kappa,\lambda)
-sequence exists.
\hfill\dashv

Clearly,
\square_{\lambda,<\kappa}
implies
\square(\kappa,\lambda^{+})
and if
\kappa\leq\kappa^{\prime}
, then
\square(\kappa,\lambda)
implies
\square(\kappa^{\prime},\lambda)
.
\square(2,\lambda)
is
\square(\lambda)
. The following is the main result of this chapter.

Theorem 12.0.2
.

Suppose
\kappa
is a cardinal such that
\kappa^{\omega}=\kappa
and
2^{2^{\aleph_{0}}}\leq\kappa
. Suppose there is a regular cardinal
\gamma\in[\omega_{2},\kappa)
such that for all

. Then there is a model
M
containing
\rm{OR}\cup\mathbb{R}
such that
M\vDash\sf{LSA}
.

We immediately have the following corollary.

Corollary 12.0.3
.

Assume one of the following theories.

1.

\sf{PFA}
.

2.

There is a strongly compact cardinal.

Then there is a model
M
containing
\rm{OR}\cup\mathbb{R}
such that
M\vDash\sf{LSA}
.

Proof.

It is well-known that (1) implies the hypothesis of Theorem

(cf.
[
68
]
); this is because
\sf{PFA}
implies
\neg\square(3,\gamma)

. The hypothesis for Theorem

.

In the previous chapter, we show

is consistent assuming the existence of a Woodin cardinal which is a limit of Woodin cardinals by analyzing the HOD of the minimal model of
\sf{LSA}

The rest of the chapter is dedicated to proving Theorem

along with the following simplifying assumption:

\kappa\textrm{ is measurable and $\forall\xi\in[\kappa,\kappa^{++}]\ 2^{\xi}=\xi^{+}$.}

(12.1)

\forall\alpha\in[\gamma,\kappa^{+4}]
,
\neg\square(3,\alpha)
.

Later, we show how to get rid of assumption

({\dagger})\ \ \

in

+\Theta=\theta_{\alpha+1}+\theta_{\alpha}

”.

Before plunging in the the details, we give a very rough outline of the proof of Theorem

. Fix

and

(\Sigma^{X}_{W})^{i}=\Sigma^{X}_{Y}
.

Proof.

Letting
Y^{*}=\tau^{X}_{W}\circ i[{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y}]
, then
{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y}={\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y^{*}}
. Moreover,
\Sigma^{X}_{Y}=\Sigma^{X}_{Y^{*}}
by Lemma
12.2.1
, and hence
\Sigma^{X}_{Y}=(\Sigma^{X}_{W})^{i}
.

An easy modification of the proof of Theorem
9.2.2
also gives us the following useful fact. A proof of this can also be found in
[
62
, Lemma 2]
. Note also that Corollary
9.1.15
is a consequence of Lemma
12.2.5
. A standard argument, using the Vopenka algebra and the fact that
{\mathcal{P}}\vDash``\delta^{\mathcal{P}}
is a regular limit of Woodin cardinals”, gives us that
L(\Omega,{\mathcal{P}})\vDash``\sf{AD}_{\mathbb{R}}+
\Theta
is regular.” See
[
62
]
for a proof.

Lemma 12.2.5
.

Suppose
X
is a condensing set. Suppose
{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathcal{R}}
are countable, transitive in
V[G]
with the property that there are elementary maps
i:{\mathcal{P}}_{X}\rightarrow{\mathcal{Q}}
,
k:{\mathcal{Q}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{R}}
,
\tau:{\mathcal{Q}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{P}}
,
\sigma:{\mathcal{R}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{P}}
such that
\tau\circ i=\pi_{X}\restriction{\mathcal{P}}_{X}
, and
\tau=\sigma\circ k
. Letting
\Sigma_{\mathcal{Q}}=\Sigma^{\tau}
and
\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}}=\Sigma^{\sigma}
, then for any
A\subseteq\delta_{X}
in
{\mathcal{P}}_{X}
and any formula
\varphi
,

L(\Omega,{\mathcal{P}})\vDash``\forall s\in{\mathcal{Q}}(\varphi[{\mathcal{Q}},s,\Sigma_{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathcal{P}},\pi_{X}(A)]\Leftrightarrow\varphi[{\mathcal{R}},k(s),\Sigma_{\mathcal{R}},{\mathcal{P}},\pi_{X}(A)])"
.

12.3
X
-suitable hod premouse and
X
-validated iterations

We summarize some key notions developed in
[
36
]
. The reader can read
[
36
]
for more details. We continue using the notations from the previous section.

Definition 12.3.1
.

Let
X
be a condensing set.
{\mathcal{Q}}

nicely extends

{\mathcal{Q}}_{X}
if
{\mathcal{Q}}
is non-meek and
{\mathcal{Q}}^{b}={\mathcal{Q}}_{X}
. We also say that
{\mathcal{Q}}
is a
nice extension
of
{\mathcal{Q}}_{X}
. Similarly, we can define what it means for
{\mathcal{Q}}
to nicely extend
{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y}
for an extension
Y
of
X
and
{\mathcal{Q}}
to nicely extend
{\mathcal{P}}
.
\hfill\dashv

Suppose
X
is a condensing set and
Y
is an extension of
X
. Suppose further that
{\mathcal{Q}}
nicely extends
{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y}
. A stack (of normal iteration trees)
{\mathcal{T}}
on
{\mathcal{Q}}
has the form

{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}=(({\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha})_{\alpha<\eta},(E_{\alpha})_{\alpha<\eta-1},D,R,(\beta_{\alpha},m_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in R},T)
,

where the displayed objects are introduced in
2.4.1
. The above notation is quite standard.
D
is the set of drops,
R
is the set of stages where player
I
starts a new round of the iteration game,
(\beta_{\alpha},m_{\alpha})
is the place player
I
drops at the beginning of the
\alpha
th round, and
T
is the tree order. Sometimes to make clear these objects are associated with
\vec{{\mathcal{T}}}
, we write
D^{\vec{{\mathcal{T}}}}
etc. Recall the convention in Chapter 2, we assume that all our stacks are proper (see Remark
2.7.27
). One of the key aspects of being proper is that if
\beta<lh({\vec{\mathcal{T}}})
is such that
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}_{\geq\beta}
is a stack on
{\mathcal{M}}^{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}_{\beta}
then
\beta\in R
4
4

4

Thus, no normal component of
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
can be split into two normal components.
. We will also use the notation introduced in
2.4.4
. In particular, for
\alpha\in R^{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
,
{\sf{next}}^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}(\alpha)=min(R^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}-(\alpha+1))
if this minimum exists and otherwise
{\sf{next}}^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}(\alpha)=lh({\vec{\mathcal{T}}})
. For
\alpha\in R^{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
, we also set
{\sf{nc}}^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}_{\alpha}={\vec{\mathcal{T}}}_{[\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}]}
where
\alpha^{\prime}={\sf{next}}^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}(\alpha)
.

Definition 12.3.2
.

Suppose
X\in Cnd({\mathcal{P}})
and
Y
is an extension of
X
. Suppose further that
{\mathcal{Q}}
nicely extends
{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y}
. Given
E\in\vec{E}^{\mathcal{Q}}
such that
{\rm crit}(E)=\delta^{{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y}}
, we say
E
is
(X,Y)
-realizable
if there is
W
, an extension of
X\oplus Y
such that
E=E^{X}_{Y,W}
, where
E^{X}_{Y,W}
is the extender defined by

(a,A)\in E^{X}_{Y,W}\Leftrightarrow\tau^{X}_{W}(a)=\pi^{\Sigma^{X}_{W}}_{{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{W},\infty}(a)\in\tau^{X}_{Y}(A),

(12.2)

for any
a\in[lh(E)]^{<\omega}
and
A\in{\wp}({\rm crit}(E))^{|a|}\cap{\mathcal{Q}}
.

We are continuing with the notation of Definition
12.3.2
. Suppose
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
is a stack on
{\mathcal{Q}}
. We say
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
is a
(X,Y)
-realizable
iteration if there is a sequence
(W_{\alpha}:\alpha\in R^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}})
such that

1.

W_{0}=Y
,

2.

if
\alpha,\beta\in R^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}
and
\alpha<\beta
then
W_{\beta}
is an extension of
X\oplus W_{\alpha}
,

3.

if
\alpha,\beta\in R^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}
,
\alpha<\beta
and
\pi^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}},b}_{\alpha,\beta}
is defined then
\pi^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}},b}_{\alpha,\beta}=\pi^{X}_{W_{\alpha},W_{\beta}}
5
5

5

The embedding
\pi^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}_{\alpha,\beta}
is defined similarly to
\pi^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}},b}
, it is essentially the embedding
\pi^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}_{\alpha,\beta}\restriction{\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha}^{b}
. See Section
2.8
.
, and

4.

if
\alpha\in R^{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
and
{\vec{\mathcal{U}}}
is the largest fragment of
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}_{\geq\alpha}
that is based on
{\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha}^{b}
then
{\vec{\mathcal{U}}}
is according to
\Psi^{X}_{W_{\alpha}}
.

We say
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
is
X
-realizable
if
Y
is an honest extension of
X
and
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
is
(X,Y)
-realizable.
\hfill\dashv

The following lemma shows that
(X,Y)
-realizability is equivalent to
X
-realizability. The proof can be found in
[
36
, Section 7]
.

Lemma 12.3.3
.

Suppose
Y
is an extension of
X
and
{\mathcal{Q}}
nicely extends
{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y}
. Suppose
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
is a
(X,Y)
-realizable iteration as witnessed by
(W^{\prime}_{\alpha}:\alpha\in R^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}})
. For
\alpha\in R^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}}
let
W_{\alpha}
be the unique honest extension of
X
with the property that
({\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha}^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}})^{b}={\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{W_{\alpha}}
. Then
(W_{\alpha}:\alpha\in R^{{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}})
witnesses that
{\mathcal{Q}}
is
X
-realizable.

We fix a condensing set
X
throughout this section. Suppose
{\mathcal{Q}}
nicely extends
{\mathcal{Q}}^{X}_{Y}
and
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
is a
X
-realizable iteration of
{\mathcal{Q}}
. We cannot in general prove that
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
picks unique branches mainly because we say nothing about
{\mathcal{Q}}
-structures that appear in

when we iterate above
\delta^{{\mathcal{S}}^{b}}
for some

and
\beta\in R^{\vec{{\mathcal{T}}}}
. The next definition introduces a notion of a premouse that resolves this issue.

Definition 12.3.4
.

We say
{\mathcal{R}}
is

X

{\mathcal{R}}
is
weakly suitable
if
{\mathcal{R}}
is a hod premouse of lsa type such that
{\mathcal{R}}=({\mathcal{R}}|\delta^{\mathcal{R}})^{\#}
,
{\mathcal{R}}
has no Woodin cardinals in the interval

, and

.
\hfill\dashv

We now define the notion of

-approved sts premouse of depth

X

Definition 12.3.5
.

We say

({\mathcal{R}})

The following facts follow straightforwardly from the definitions above (see

Definition 12.3.8

We say that a weakly

Note that in the above definition, for each

Proposition 12.3.9
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{R}}
is a weakly

-suitable hod premouse that is not infinitely descending and

Proof.

The proof easily follows from results of Section 4, particularly Lemma

, and Section 9.2. Suppose first that

(a)

if
{\vec{\mathcal{T}}}
doesn’t have a last component or

(b)

In case (a), there is nothing to prove. In case (b), let

7
7

7

Notice that in this case there is a branch

Corollary 12.7.9
.

Suppose
Y\prec Z\prec{\mathcal{M}}_{\xi}
are countable (in
V[G]
), and such that

are honest extensions of
X
,
Y,Z\in V
, and
Y=Y^{*}\cap{\mathcal{M}}_{\xi}
,

for some

. Let
\pi_{Y,Z}=\pi_{Z}^{-1}\circ\pi_{Y}
. Then
\Sigma^{Y}_{\xi}=(\Sigma^{Z}_{\xi})^{\pi_{Y,Z}}
.

Proof.

Let
\delta_{Y}=\pi_{Y}^{-1}(\delta^{\mathcal{P}})
and
\delta_{Z}=\pi_{Z}^{-1}(\delta^{\mathcal{P}})
. By our assumption on
Y
and
Z
, we have:

\pi_{Z}\restriction\delta_{Z}=\pi^{\Sigma^{Z}_{\xi}}_{{\mathcal{N}}^{Z}_{\xi},\infty}\restriction\delta_{Z}
,

and

\pi_{Y}\restriction\delta_{Y}=\pi^{\Sigma^{Y}_{\xi}}_{{\mathcal{N}}^{Y}_{\xi},\infty}\restriction\delta_{Y}=\pi_{Z}\circ\pi_{Y,Z}\restriction\delta_{Y}
.

Using the above equations and the proof of Lemma
12.7.6
(especially the idea that if two strategies disagree, then there is a lower-level disagreement), we obtain the desired conclusion.

Claim 12.7.17

For

Now,

\displaystyle(a,A)\in\tilde{F}^{Y}

\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow

\displaystyle(\tau(a)=\pi^{Y}(a),A)\in F^{Y}_{\xi}

\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow

By what has been shown, the comparison does not encounter strategy disagreements. The point is that since
\Psi
is a
\tau
-realizable strategy and
X\subset\textrm{rng}(\tau)
, it witnesses that
\Psi
-iterates of
({\mathcal{M}}^{*})^{Y}
are
X
-approved. A similar comment applies to the the canonical strategy of
{\mathcal{R}}^{Y}
.

\xi
-sound and
{\mathcal{R}}^{Y}
is a
{\mathcal{Q}}
-structure for

,
({\mathcal{M}}^{*})^{Y}\unlhd{\mathcal{R}}^{Y}
. This implies
{\mathcal{M}}^{*}\lhd{\mathcal{N}}_{\Upsilon}
.

(ii) follows from the fact that
{\mathcal{M}}^{*}
is an initial segment of a model in a hybrid

-construction that produces

. Furthermore, since there is a
{\mathcal{Q}}

for

(iii) follows from an argument as in Corolloary

; the main point is that by Lemmata

and

, letting

be

are certified. More precisely, let

be the tree on the
{\mathcal{M}}^{Y}
-side that participate in the comparison. Suppose
{\mathcal{R}}={\mathcal{M}}^{\mathcal{S}}_{\alpha}
and

and that
{\mathcal{S}}\restriction\alpha
,
{\mathcal{T}}\restriction\alpha
have not used extenders with critical point

. Suppose

is the largest such that

. Since no strategy disagreement occurs by Lemma

For (iv), the point is that in the relevant phalanx comparisons in the proof of solidity and universality, no extenders with critical point
(\delta^{{\mathcal{P}}})^{Y}
are used by (iii), no strategy disagreements occur, and hence these comparisons are successful.

Suppose without loss of generality, no countable substructures of any

.

Again, Lemma
12.8.3
and results in Section 8.2 show that the new derived model of
{\mathcal{N}}
as in the conclusion of Lemma

(at the sup of its Woodin cardinals) satisfies

Now by boolean comparisons, there is some
({\mathcal{M}},\Sigma)\in V
satisfying Definition
8.2.2
. By taking a countable hull of
{\mathcal{M}}

Proof of Theorem
12.0.2
.
The arguments above prove the consistency of
\sf{LSA}
from the hypothesis of Theorem
12.0.2
plus the simplifying assumption (
12.1
). For this argument, since
2^{<\kappa}=\kappa
and the core model induction is carried out in
V^{Coll(\omega,<\kappa)}
,
\sf{ord}
({\mathcal{P}})<\kappa^{+}
as shown in Lemma
12.1.2
. The constructions on top of
{\mathcal{P}}
go on for at most
\kappa^{+++}
many steps and the hypothesis we need to carry out the arguments in the previous sections is
\forall\alpha\in[\gamma,\kappa^{+4}]\ \neg\square(3,\alpha)
.

To eliminate (
12.1
), we carry out the core model induction in
V^{Coll(\omega,\kappa)}
much like that in
[
67
]
to obtain objects like
\Gamma,{\mathcal{P}}
. We note that in this case, using the argument in
12.1.2
, we can show
\sf{ord}
({\mathcal{P}}^{-})\leq(2^{\kappa})^{+}
and
\sf{ord}
({\mathcal{P}})<(2^{\kappa})^{++}
. Now similar to the proof of
[
12
, Theorem 4.1]
, letting
\xi=2^{\kappa}
,
\mathbb{P}=Coll(\omega,\kappa)\star Coll(\xi^{+},\xi^{+})\star Coll(\xi^{++},\xi^{++})\star Coll(\xi^{+++},\xi^{+++})
, we carry out the hybrid
K^{c}
-constructions and the
X
-validated sts constructions over
{\mathcal{P}}
in
V^{\mathbb{P}}
. By homogeneity, the objects constructed are in
V
. We use Theorem
9.2.15
, which in turns was built on
9.2.14
,
9.2.13
, and
9.2.11
, to obtain condensing sets and adapt the constructions in the previous sections of this chapter to obtain a model of
\sf{LSA}
in a straightforward way. Note that in
V^{\mathbb{P}}
,
\xi^{+++}
is countably closed and
2^{<\xi^{+++}}=\xi^{+++}
; this allows the proof of Lemma
12.6.2
to go through in this case. The constructions above
{\mathcal{P}}
in the previous sections go on for at most
\xi^{+++}
many steps and we need the full hypothesis
\forall\alpha\in[\gamma,({\wp}_{4}(\kappa)^{+}]\ \neg\square(3,\alpha)
to carry out the arguments.
56
56

56

In
V^{\mathbb{P}}
,
{\wp}_{1}^{V}(\xi)
is collapsed to
\xi^{+}
,
{\wp}_{2}^{V}(\xi)
is collapsed to
\xi^{++}
, and
{\wp}_{3}^{V}(\xi)
is collapsed to
\xi^{+++}
. It seems very plausible that Lemma
12.6.2
can be proven with less than what we assumed, but we have not checked this thoroughly.
We leave the details to the kind reader.

and
Z^{\kappa}\subset Z
.
